sections.title: Human language and computation
Speech movements in MRI

teaching.text: **Real-time magnetic resonance imaging (real-time MRI)** records a moving picture of the inside of a person's head and neck while they talk. The view is taken from the side, as if the head were cut straight down the middle from the forehead to the chin, so the face points to the left and the back of the neck is on the right. Air shows up black. Soft tissue such as the tongue, lips, and throat walls shows up in shades of gray and white. This method lets us watch structures move that are normally hidden inside the body.
children: The **lips** sit at the far left edge, and they open, close, round, and spread during speech.

The **tongue** is the large rounded gray mass that fills most of the mouth. It is the most active structure in speech, and it changes shape constantly, bunching up toward the roof of the mouth, pulling back toward the throat, or lying low.

The **roof of the mouth** runs above the tongue. Its front part is the hard, bony **hard palate.** Its back part is the soft, movable **soft palate,** also called the **velum,** which can lift to seal off the nose or lower to let air flow out through the nose.

Behind the tongue, a dark vertical channel of air runs down the throat. This is the **pharynx.** Below it sits the **larynx,** which holds the **vocal folds,** and behind all of it the bright vertical column of the spine runs down the right side of the image.

teaching.text: When a person speaks, all of these structures move at the same time and at high speed. The jaw rises and falls, the lips open and close, the tongue reshapes itself many times per second, and the soft palate lifts and lowers. Each sound we make depends on a precise shape of this whole passage, and the shapes follow one another smoothly rather than one at a time. The two MRI movies capture the same speaker's vocal tract in two different shapes, and the difference between them comes almost entirely from where the tongue and lips are placed.

sections.title: Why speech is a remarkable learned skill

teaching.text: We learn to move our speech organs in extremely complex ways with no instructions and with almost no visual feedback. Nobody tells a young child where to place the tongue tip for a particular sound or how high to lift the back of the tongue. A child also cannot see their own tongue, soft palate, or vocal folds, since these are hidden inside the mouth and throat in exactly the way the MRI images reveal. Even so, children master these movements.

**By ages 2 to 4,** children speak with a wide vocabulary and with language that is close to adult language. This happens with hardly any explicit instruction. Children are not given lessons in grammar or pronunciation at this age, yet they pick up thousands of words and the rules for putting them together just from being around people who talk.

**Reading and writing** follow a very different path. A child may memorize the visual shapes of the letters of the alphabet fairly early. Reading and writing whole words, though, usually comes at **ages 6 to 7,** and it requires a great deal of instruction.
children: The contrast is striking. Speech involves hidden organs that the learner cannot see, yet it develops almost on its own.
Reading and writing involve the eyes and hands, which are fully visible, yet they need years of deliberate teaching.
This difference shows that speech is a deep human cognitive skill that the brain is prepared to acquire, while literacy is a learned tool built on top of it.

teaching.text: **Articulatory phonetics** is the field that studies the movements of the different structures of the vocal tract. The **vocal tract** is the full air passage used in speech, running from the larynx up through the throat and mouth to the lips, with a side branch into the nose. Articulatory phonetics asks which structures move, where they move to, and how those movements create the different sounds of a language. Real-time MRI is one of the main tools of this field, since it lets researchers measure the tongue, lips, and soft palate directly while a person talks.

In just the **last two years, voice assistants** and other **speech technology** have come to **emulate** human speech ability in ways that almost no one thought possible. To emulate an ability means to reproduce its behavior. These systems can now produce speech that sounds natural and humanlike, and they can recognize and respond to spoken language with high accuracy.

**LING 285 is about both human speech and AI speech.** One side of the course studies how people physically produce and perceive speech. The other side studies how modern AI systems model that same ability, so the human skill and the machine version can be compared directly.

sections.title: Air vibration and acoustic phonetics

teaching.text: The next step in understanding speech is to focus not on the tongue and lips themselves but on the **air** that fills the space between the tongue and the rest of the vocal tract. In the real vocal tract, that air space bends: it runs down the throat and then turns forward through the mouth. If we ignore that curve and straighten the passage out, the vocal tract becomes a simple **tube of air.**
children: One end of the tube corresponds to the **lips,** where the passage is open to the outside air.
The other end corresponds to the **larynx** deep in the throat, where the tube is treated as closed.
The walls of the tube stand for the tongue and the other surfaces that surround the air space.

teaching.text: The tube is labeled **schwa.** Schwa is the neutral, relaxed vowel sound, the "uh" sound in the first syllable of "about" or the last syllable of "sofa." For schwa, the tongue sits in a central resting position and does not narrow the passage much anywhere, so the air space is close to the same width from end to end. That makes schwa the vowel that fits the straight, even tube best.

Inside the tube, the air is drawn as many small blue circles arranged in vertical columns, and each circle stands for a small bit of air. When the tube vibrates, these bits of air do not travel down the tube and out the end. Instead, each column shifts back and forth around its own resting position.
children: As neighboring columns move toward each other, the air in that region is squeezed together into a **compression,** where the air is packed more tightly.
As neighboring columns move away from each other, the air in that region spreads out into a **rarefaction,** where the air is packed more loosely.
These regions of packing and spreading move along the tube and reflect back from its ends, and this repeating pattern is the **vibration of air** that makes up the sound of the vowel.

teaching.text: **Acoustic phonetics** is the field that studies exactly this: how air vibrates in the vocal tract and what sound those vibrations produce. Articulatory phonetics describes the shape of the tube, and acoustic phonetics describes the physics of the air inside it. The two fields connect directly, since changing the tongue and lip positions changes the shape of the tube, and changing the shape of the tube changes how the air inside it vibrates.

sections.title: Why scientific understanding of AI matters

teaching.text: AI brings real **psychological, economic, social, and environmental harms.** Given everything known about these harms, it is tempting to simply ignore AI and act as if it did not exist. Many scientists also warn about **existential harm,** meaning the possibility that advanced AI could threaten humanity's survival or basic way of life. Even with that warning, pretending AI does not exist is not a workable option.

AI exists, and it comes with many harms and also some benefits. Two examples of benefits are **immunotherapy,** a medical approach that uses the body's own immune system to fight diseases such as cancer, and **environmental engineering,** the design of solutions to environmental problems.
children: The environmental case cuts both ways, as captured by a newspaper headline asking, **"Will A.I. Ruin the Planet or Save the Planet?"**
Running large AI systems uses enormous amounts of energy, which is one of the environmental harms, while AI tools are also being applied to engineering problems that could help the environment.

teaching.text: One of the biggest dangers of AI is that **we have no idea how it works.** This is summed up in the phrase **"We know everything, and understand nothing."**
children: "We know everything" means that every number and every calculation inside an AI system is available to be inspected, since people built the system and can look at all of its parts.
"We understand nothing" means that, even with all of those details in hand, no one can explain why the system produces the particular answers it does or what it is really doing when it produces them.

teaching.text: The number of people who **know** how these systems operate is very, very small. That concentration of knowledge is a danger in itself, since the decisions about how AI is built and used end up in very few hands.

**AI literacy,** meaning a working understanding of what AI systems are and how they behave, is necessary for many groups of people. Scientists who use AI need it to judge whether their results are trustworthy. Politicians who need to control AI need it to write sensible rules. Lawyers who litigate cases involving AI need it to argue about what a system did and why.

This course is built on the belief that a **creative thinker** in a class like this one can help us understand these systems well enough to benefit from them while avoiding their negative consequences. Understanding is the path to both getting the benefits and limiting the harms.

sections.title: Course goals

teaching.text: The course has four **specific goals.**
children: The first is to appreciate the human cognitive skill of **speech,** the complex ability described in the MRI images and the learning timeline, which people acquire with almost no instruction.
The second is to understand some basic principles of **physics** through speech, such as the way air vibrates inside the tube of the vocal tract.
The third is to understand how modern **AI systems model human cognition,** meaning how machines reproduce abilities such as speaking and understanding language.

The fourth is to sharpen **methodical reasoning** through **elementary programming.** Writing simple programs forces each step of a problem to be stated clearly and in the correct order, which trains careful, step-by-step thinking.

teaching.text: The course also has three **general goals.**
children: The first is learning to think creatively in a rich **interdisciplinary** way. The material draws on physics, psychology, linguistics, biology, economics, computer science, philosophy, neuroscience, and many other fields. Speech alone already touches several of these, since it involves the biology of the vocal tract, the physics of vibrating air, the psychology of learning, and the neuroscience of how the brain controls movement.
The second is deepening our understanding of the world we are all living in today, a world in which AI systems are becoming part of daily life.
The third is sharpening our **skillful use of modern AI systems,** so that we use them well and with a clear sense of what they can and cannot do.

sections.title: Moving from memorization to creative reasoning

teaching.text: **Diotima,** dated here to around 440 **BCE,** is the teacher who, in Plato's dialogue the Symposium, teaches **Socrates** about a ladder of ascent. The ladder describes how a person climbs from ordinary, surface-level knowledge of particular things toward deeper understanding of the general ideas behind them. A chain of teachers runs from her through Greek philosophy: Diotima taught Socrates, Socrates taught **Plato,** and Plato taught **Aristotle.** The large marble bust represents Diotima, and the three smaller portraits below her represent Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle in that order.
The **bottom of the ladder** holds the kinds of knowledge and skill that come from routine and from copying what already exists.
children: These include **daily experience, habit,** and **memorization,** along with **specialized skills, repetition and replication,** and learning from **textbooks.**

Thinking at this level follows the rule that **similar is same, and slight difference is different.** Things that look alike on the surface are treated as identical, and things that look even a little different on the surface are treated as unrelated.

teaching.text: The **top of the ladder** holds **creativity, insight, thought, focus, attention, imagination, and vision,** along with **problem-posing, problem-solving, critical reading, and creative writing.**
children: Thinking at this level follows a reversed rule: **different can be same, and similar can be different.** Things that look different on the surface can share the same deeper structure, and things that look alike on the surface can turn out to be fundamentally different.

Speech gives a direct example. The sounds f and v sound different, yet they are made in the same place in the mouth, so in that respect they are the same. The th in "thing" and the th in "that" are spelled identically, yet one uses vocal fold vibration and the other does not, so they are different sounds.
**Problem-posing** means asking good questions in the first place, which is separate from **problem-solving,** which means answering questions once they have been asked.

teaching.text: A person climbs the ladder through repeated cycles of **question and answer.** Each cycle of asking a question and working out an answer lifts understanding one rung higher, and the cycles repeat again and again on the way from the bottom to the top. This is the method Socrates became famous for, and it traces back to Diotima's teaching of him.

For about 2500 **years,** people could fake it. They could do well in school and at work without ever climbing the ladder, simply by memorizing, repeating, and replicating. In 2026 that is no longer true. In interviews for jobs and for graduate school, what matters now is whether a person shows the properties at the **top of Diotima's ladder,** such as creativity, insight, problem-posing, and the ability to see when different things are the same and similar things are different.

sections.title: Voicing and place through sustained fricatives

teaching.text: The quickest way to understand speech sounds is to produce them and pay attention to what the body does. The exercise uses four pairs of sounds, and each pair is held out as one long continuous sound that switches partway through from the first sound to the second.
children: The first pair is **f then v.** Say the f in "fat" and hold it, then switch to the v in "vat" and hold that.
The second pair is **th then th.** Say the th in "thing" and hold it, then switch to the th in "that" and hold that.
The third pair is **s then z.** Say the s in "sing" and hold it, then switch to the z in "zing" and hold that.

The fourth pair is **sh then j.** Say the sh in "mesh" and hold it, then switch to the sound written j here, which is the sound in the middle of "beige." This is the soft buzzing sound, not the j in "jump."

teaching.text: The first question is what changes between the first and second sound of each pair. Resting the fingers lightly on the front of the throat while switching makes the change easy to feel.
children: During f, the first th, s, and sh, the throat stays still and the sound is a pure hiss of air.
During v, the second th, z, and the sound in "beige," a buzzing vibration appears in the throat and the sound gains a humming quality.

The difference is **voice,** which is whether the **vocal folds** vibrate or not. The vocal folds are two small folds of tissue inside the larynx. When they are held apart, air passes through silently and the sound is **voiceless.** When they are brought close together, the air flowing between them makes them vibrate rapidly, and the sound is **voiced.**
Within each pair, the tongue and lips stay in the same position the whole time. Only the vocal folds change, which shows that voicing is controlled separately from the mouth.

teaching.text: The second question is what changes from one line to the next, meaning from the f and v pair to the th pair to the s and z pair to the sh pair.
children: For f and v, the lower lip presses lightly against the upper front teeth.
For both th sounds, the tip of the tongue touches the upper front teeth.
For s and z, the tip of the tongue comes close to the ridge just behind the upper front teeth.
For sh and the sound in "beige," the tongue pulls a bit further back, behind that ridge.

The difference is **place of articulation,** which is the location in the vocal tract where the narrowing that makes the sound is formed. Moving from one line to the next moves that narrowing steadily further back in the mouth.

teaching.text: Voice and place of articulation are two separate, independent properties of a speech sound. Every sound in this exercise can be described by stating both of them, and changing one while keeping the other fixed produces a different sound.

sections.title: The fricative system

teaching.text: All of the sounds in the exercise belong to a group called **fricatives.** A fricative is made by bringing two parts of the vocal tract very close together without closing the passage completely. Air pushed from the lungs is forced through the narrow gap, and passing through such a small opening makes the air flow turbulent and chaotic. That turbulent flow produces the hissing or buzzing noise that is typical of fricatives, and the sound can be held for as long as there is breath.
The English fricatives are organized in a table by **voice** in the rows and **place of articulation** in the columns.
children: **Labial Dental Alveolar Postalveolar**

teaching.text: **Voiceless** f th s sh
**Voiced** v th z j
Each column is a place of articulation, and each column contains one voiceless and one voiced fricative made in that same place.
children: **Labial** means made with the lips. For f and v, the lower lip rises to lightly touch the upper front teeth, and the air hisses through the gaps between them. Real- time MRI of these sounds shows the lower lip tucked up under the upper teeth while the tongue lies relatively low and relaxed in the mouth.

**Dental** means made at the teeth. For the th in "thing" and the th in "that," the tip of the tongue touches or rests just between the upper front teeth. The MRI of these sounds shows the front of the tongue pushed forward right up to the teeth.

**Alveolar** means made at the **alveolar ridge,** the small bony ridge on the roof of the mouth just behind the upper front teeth. For s and z, the tongue tip rises to form a narrow groove close to that ridge. The MRI shows the tongue tip raised toward the front of the roof of the mouth, a short distance behind the teeth.

**Postalveolar** means made just behind the alveolar ridge. For sh and the sound in "beige," a wider section of the front of the tongue rises toward the roof of the mouth a little further back than for s. The MRI shows the raised part of the tongue shifted backward compared with s, and the lips often push slightly forward during these sounds.

teaching.text: Each row is a voicing category. The top row holds the **voiceless** fricatives, made with the vocal folds apart and still. The bottom row holds the **voiced** fricatives, made with the vocal folds vibrating. Two fricatives in the same column differ only in voicing, and two fricatives in the same row differ only in place of articulation. The two th sounds make the point sharply, since English spells them the same way even though one is voiceless and the other is voiced.

sections.title: Stop place, voicing, and nasality

teaching.text: **Stops** are made differently from fricatives. For a stop, two parts of the vocal tract come together and **close the passage completely,** so that for a brief moment air cannot escape through the mouth at all.
children: While the closure is held, air coming up from the lungs keeps pushing into the mouth, and the air pressure builds up behind the closure.
When the closure is released, the trapped air bursts out suddenly, and that burst is part of what makes a stop sound short and sharp.
Unlike a fricative, a stop cannot be held as a continuous sound, since the sound depends on the closing and the release.

teaching.text: The English stops fall into a grid of three places of articulation and three types. Real-time MRI movies capture each of these nine sounds in the middle of its closure.
The first row is **p, b, and m,** and all three are made by closing the **lips.**
children: For p, the lips press together, the vocal folds stay still, and the release produces a voiceless puff of air.
For b, the lips close in the same way, but the vocal folds vibrate, so b is voiced.

For m, the lips close in the same way and the vocal folds vibrate, but the **soft palate lowers.** This opens the passage into the nose, so air flows out through the nose the whole time the lips are closed. A sound made this way is called a **nasal,** and the MRI of m shows the gap opened between the soft palate and the back of the throat.

teaching.text: The second row is **t, d, and n,** and all three are made by pressing the tip of the tongue against the **alveolar ridge,** the same place used for s and z.
children: For t, the tongue tip seals against the ridge and the vocal folds stay still, so t is voiceless.
For d, the tongue tip seals in the same place and the vocal folds vibrate, so d is voiced.

For n, the tongue tip seals in the same place, the vocal folds vibrate, and the soft palate lowers so air escapes through the nose, which makes n a nasal. The MRI images of this row show the front of the tongue raised and pressed against the roof of the mouth just behind the teeth.

teaching.text: The third row is **k, g, and ng,** and all three are made by raising the **back of the tongue** against the **soft palate** at the back of the roof of the mouth.
children: For k, the back of the tongue seals against the soft palate and the vocal folds stay still, so k is voiceless.
For g, the seal is in the same place and the vocal folds vibrate, so g is voiced.

For ng, the sound at the end of "sing," the seal is in the same place, the vocal folds vibrate, and the passage to the nose opens so air flows out through the nose. The MRI images of this row show the tongue bunched upward and backward, meeting the roof of the mouth far back near the throat, while the lips and tongue tip stay out of the way.

teaching.text: The columns of the grid follow the same logic as the fricative table. The first column, **p, t, and k,** holds the **voiceless** stops. The second column, **b, d, and g,** holds the **voiced** stops. The third column, **m, n, and ng,** holds the **nasal** stops, which are voiced and send air through the nose. Reading down a column changes only the place of articulation, from the lips to the alveolar ridge to the soft palate. Reading across a row keeps the place fixed and changes only voicing and whether the nose is open. Nine different sounds come from combining just three places of closure with three settings of the vocal folds and soft palate, which shows how a small number of independent movements builds a large set of speech sounds.

lecture02.title: 02 · Speech structure and learning in AI

sections.title: Human language and technology
Lecture agenda
Internal coordination during speech

teaching.text: **Real-time** MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) lets us film the inside of the head while a person is talking. The images are **midsagittal,** which means they are a side-view slice taken straight down the middle of the head, from the nose to the back of the neck. The face points to the left, so the lips are on the left edge and the spinal column is the bright vertical band on the right. The recordings run for about half a minute each and include the sound of the speaker, so every movement can be matched to the speech it produces.
children: In MRI, **air shows up black** because it gives off almost no signal, and soft tissue like the tongue shows up gray or white. The dark spaces in the image are therefore the open airways: the mouth cavity, the nasal passages above the roof of the mouth, and the **pharynx,** which is the air tube at the back of the throat behind the tongue.

The large rounded gray mass filling most of the mouth is the **tongue.** Above it is the **hard palate,** the bony roof of the mouth, and hanging down from the back of the hard palate is the **velum,** or soft palate, which can be raised or lowered to close or open the path from the throat into the nose.

teaching.text: When these recordings play, the tongue, lips, jaw, and velum are all moving at once and very quickly. Every consonant and vowel we hear is the result of the speaker shaping this tube of air in a particular way. **Phonetics** is the study of these speech sounds, and the images give us a direct way to see the shapes behind them.

sections.title: Fricative place and voicing

teaching.text: A **fricative** is a consonant made by bringing two parts of the mouth very close together without closing them completely. Air is pushed through that narrow gap, and the squeezed air becomes turbulent, which produces the hissing or buzzing noise we hear in sounds like f and s. A fricative can be held for as long as we have breath, which is different from sounds that require a full closure.

English fricatives are organized along two dimensions: **place of articulation** and **voicing.** Place of articulation is where in the mouth the narrow gap is formed. Voicing is whether the **vocal folds** in the larynx are vibrating while the sound is made.
children: A **voiceless** sound is made with the vocal folds apart and not vibrating, so the only noise is the hiss of air through the gap.

A **voiced** sound is made with the vocal folds vibrating, so the hiss is combined with a buzz. Placing a hand on the throat while saying "ssss" and then "zzzz" makes the difference easy to feel, since only the second produces vibration.

teaching.text: The English fricatives fall into **four places of articulation,** and each place has a voiceless and a voiced member.
children: **Labial** fricatives are f (voiceless) and v (voiced). The word labial refers to the lips, and for f and v the lower lip is raised up against the upper front teeth.

**Dental** fricatives are both spelled th. The voiceless one is the sound at the start of "think," and the voiced one is the sound at the start of "this." The tip of the tongue is placed against or just between the upper teeth.
**Alveolar** fricatives are s (voiceless) and z (voiced). The **alveolar ridge** is the bony ridge just behind the upper front teeth, and the tongue tip is raised close to it.

**Postalveolar** fricatives are sh (voiceless) and the voiced partner symbolized as j, which is the sound in the middle of "measure" and "vision." The narrow gap is formed just behind the alveolar ridge, a little farther back in the mouth than for s and z.

teaching.text: The four MRI images line up with these four places, and they show how the constriction moves backward from one place to the next.
children: In the labial image, the lower lip is pulled up toward the upper teeth while the tongue stays low and relaxed in the mouth.
In the dental image, the front of the tongue is pushed forward toward the teeth.
In the alveolar image, the tongue tip is raised up toward the ridge behind the upper teeth.
In the postalveolar image, the narrowing sits slightly farther back, with more of the front part of the tongue raised toward the roof of the mouth.

teaching.text: The pairing matters: f and v, the two th sounds, s and z, and sh and its voiced partner are each made with the **same place and the same manner.** The only thing that separates the members of each pair is whether the vocal folds are vibrating.

sections.title: Oral and nasal stop comparisons

teaching.text: A **stop** is a consonant made by closing the vocal tract completely at some point so that air cannot get out through the mouth. Air pressure builds up behind the closure, and when the closure is released, the trapped air bursts out. English has two kinds of stops, **oral stops** and **nasal stops.**
children: In an **oral stop,** also called a **plosive,** the velum is raised and presses against the back wall of the throat, which seals off the nose. With both the mouth and the nose closed, pressure builds and is released as a small burst of air.

In a **nasal stop,** the mouth is closed in exactly the same way, but the velum is lowered. Air flows up and out through the nose the whole time, so there is no pressure build-up, and the sound has a humming quality.

teaching.text: The stops are grouped into **three places of articulation,** and each place has a voiceless oral stop, a voiced oral stop, and a nasal stop.
children: At the **lips,** p is voiceless, b is voiced, and m is the nasal. The MRI images for p, b, and m all show the two lips pressed together, closing off the front of the mouth.
At the **alveolar ridge,** t is voiceless, d is voiced, and n is the nasal. The images for t, d, and n show the tip of the tongue raised and pressed against the ridge behind the upper teeth.

At the **velum,** k is voiceless, g is voiced, and ng is the nasal, which is the sound at the end of "sing." A sound made at the velum is called **velar.** The images for k, g, and ng show the back of the tongue humped up and pressed against the soft palate.

teaching.text: The nasal images differ from the oral images in the position of the velum. In m, n, and ng, the velum hangs down away from the back of the throat, leaving an open passage into the nose, while in p, t, and k the velum is raised to seal that passage. The short video clips of each stop show the closure forming and releasing in real time, which makes it clear that a stop is an event in time: first closure, then pressure or nasal airflow, then release.

sections.title: Three dimensions of consonant knowledge

teaching.text: The fricatives and stops fit together into one table built on three properties: **manner of articulation, place of articulation,** and **voice.** Manner of articulation is how the air is shaped, whether through a narrow gap as in a fricative, a full closure with the nose sealed as in an oral stop, or a full closure with the nose open as in a nasal stop.
children: The places run from the front of the mouth to the back: **labial, dental, alveolar, postalveolar,** and **velar.**
The fricatives fill the labial, dental, alveolar, and postalveolar columns, each with a voiceless and voiced member: f and v, th and th, s and z, and sh and j.
The oral stops fill the labial, alveolar, and velar columns: voiceless p, t, and k, and voiced b, d, and g.
The nasal stops fill the same three columns as the oral stops, and all of them are voiced: m, n, and ng.

teaching.text: Every one of these consonants can be described by a combination of three values. For example, t is a **voiceless alveolar oral stop,** and z is a **voiced alveolar fricative.** Changing just one value produces a different sound: changing t from voiceless to voiced gives d, and changing d from an oral stop to a nasal stop gives n.

The empty cells are also informative. None of these English consonants is a dental or postalveolar stop, and none is a velar fricative. The sounds of English are therefore not a random collection of noises but a **highly structured system** of shared properties.

Every English speaker already uses this system every time they talk, without ever having been taught the table. This means a speaker's knowledge of English contains a great deal of hidden structure, organized along place, manner, and voice.

sections.title: AI as a model of psychological abilities

teaching.text: **Artificial intelligence (AI)** is a model of several **psychological skills that animals have.** The five skills are **knowing, recognizing, attending, acting,** and **learning.**
children: Knowing is having information stored in a usable form.
Recognizing is identifying something from the input that arrives.
Attending is selecting which parts of the input to focus on.
Acting is producing a behavior or output.
Learning is changing over time based on experience.

teaching.text: The way AI models each of these skills is **at least slightly based on how humans perform them.** This goes against a common view that AI is purely a technical innovation that appeared out of nowhere. AI grew out of ideas about human and animal psychology, and each part of an AI system can be traced back to a human skill it was built to imitate.

sections.title: Taylor’s cloze procedure

teaching.text: The question of how AI **knows** something connects to a 1953 paper by **Wilson** L. **Taylor** titled **"Cloze Procedure": A New Tool for Measuring Readability.** It was published in the Fall 1953 issue of **Journalism Quarterly,** a journal devoted to research studies in the field of mass communications.
children: The paper was the first comprehensive statement of a research method and its theory, which had been introduced briefly during a workshop at the 1953 **AEJ convention.**

It reported findings from **three pilot studies and two experiments** in which cloze procedure results were compared with the results of two existing **readability formulas,** which are formulas that estimate how easy a piece of writing is to read.

teaching.text: Taylor described **cloze procedure** as a new **psychological tool for measuring the effectiveness of communication.** The method is straightforward, the data are easily turned into numbers, and the findings held up in testing.
children: At first the tool was treated as a new approach to **readability,** and it was used that way in the three pilot studies and two experiments.

Its results were repeatedly shown to agree with two standard devices for estimating readability, the **Flesch** and **Dale-Chall** formulas. After that, cloze procedure was tested directly against those standard formulas.
Taylor expected that if future research supported these results, the tool would have many theoretical and practical uses in other fields that involve communication.

teaching.text: Taylor credited **Prof. Charles E. Osgood** of the University of Illinois and **Melvin** R. **Marks** of the Personnel Research Section, A.G.O., Department of the Army, for starting and helping with the work that produced the idea of cloze procedure. Both were **experimental psychologists.**
children: Others who advised or helped included **Prof. Lee** J. **Cronbach,** an educational psychologist and statistician; **Dean Wilbur Schramm** of the Division of Communications; **Prof. Charles E. Swanson** of the Institute of Communications Research; and **George** R. **Klare,** a psychologist. Both Swanson and Klare had written articles on readability.
**Kalmer E. Stordahl** and **Clifford** M. **Christensen,** research associates of the Institute, also contributed, along with several journalism teachers who let their classes take part.

teaching.text: The origin of cloze procedure in experimental psychology is important for AI. A tool built to measure human understanding of language ended up describing what it means for a system to know something.

sections.title: Closure turns incomplete input into a whole pattern

teaching.text: At the center of Taylor's method is a unit of measurement called a **cloze.** It is pronounced like the verb "close," and the name comes from the word **closure.**
children: **Closure** is a term from **Gestalt psychology,** the branch of psychology that studies how we perceive whole patterns. It refers to the human tendency to **complete a familiar pattern that is not quite finished.**
The standard example is a broken circle. We tend to see a circle with a gap as a whole circle, filling in the missing piece in our minds.

teaching.text: The black shapes next to Taylor's text show closure in action. There are three black circles, each with a wedge cut out of it, and the wedges all point inward toward a common center. Nothing in the picture is actually a triangle, yet we see a bright white triangle sitting on top of the three circles, with edges that seem to run between the cut-out wedges. The visual system completes the triangle from the partial information the wedges provide.
Taylor explained that a person can complete a broken circle because its shape is **so familiar** that it can be recognized even when much of it is missing. The same principle applies to language.
children: Given the sentence "Chickens cackle and ___ quack," almost anyone can instantly supply the word "ducks."
If the word a person supplies is the same as the word that was removed, that person scores **one cloze unit** for correctly closing the gap in the language pattern.

teaching.text: Filling that single blank requires a surprising amount of knowledge. The sentence is a complex pattern built out of many smaller patterns.
children: A reader must know the **meanings** of all five words, which Taylor describes as patterns of relationships between symbols and meanings.
A reader must also know their **forms,** meaning the patterns of letters that make up each word.
Beyond single words, a reader must know the meanings of **combinations** of words.

The reader must also notice that the sentence is built in two parallel halves. The first half pairs an animal with its sound, "chickens cackle," so the second half calls for the animal that goes with the sound "quack."
In other words, a reader has to guess what the incomplete sentence means as a whole and then complete its pattern to fit that whole meaning.

teaching.text: Taylor gave two formal definitions.
children: A **cloze unit** is any single occurrence of a **successful attempt to reproduce accurately a part deleted from a "message",** where a message is any language product, by deciding from the context that remains what the missing part should be.

**Cloze procedure** is a method of **intercepting a message from a "transmitter",** which is a writer or speaker, **mutilating its language patterns by deleting parts,** and giving the damaged message to **"receivers",** who are readers or listeners. The receivers' attempts to make the patterns whole again produce a large number of cloze units, which can be counted.

sections.title: What successful completion requires

teaching.text: AI shows that it knows something by **demonstrating the ability to complete, or cloze, sequences.** A system that can reliably fill in the missing parts of language has captured the patterns of that language.

The same kind of test works for people. A teacher can test a student's knowledge of a skill by asking the student to complete some sequence, such as finishing a sentence, supplying the next step in a procedure, or filling in a missing word. Success at completion is taken as evidence of knowledge.

AI takes this idea to its limit. From the AI point of view, **knowledge is nothing more than completion.** A system counts as knowing English if, given part of an English sequence, it can correctly produce what comes next or what is missing, and no further ingredient beyond that ability is required.

sections.title: From words to vectors and next-word probabilities

teaching.text: **GPT** is a system that takes in a sequence of words and predicts what word should come next. The words themselves are the input, so the first question is what a word looks like to a computer.

To a computer, a word is simply **a bunch of random numbers.** Each word in the vocabulary is assigned its own set of numbers, and the only strict requirement at the start is that **no two words share the same set of numbers.** The numbers do not need to mean anything at first, as long as each word can be told apart from every other word.
A list of numbers like this is called a **vector.** The vector for a single word could contain 1024 **numbers.**
children: In the diagram, the words "chickens," "cackle," "and," and "ducks" are each drawn as a tall vertical bar. Each bar stands for one vector, a column of 1024 numbers that represents that word.
The input to GPT is therefore not letters or sounds but a row of vectors, one for each word in the sequence.

teaching.text: Given the sequence "chickens cackle and ducks ___," a system that **knows English** will produce an output vector of 10,000 **numbers.** Each of those numbers is the **probability that a particular word of English could be the next word.**
children: In the diagram, this output is drawn as one long horizontal bar, with labels for a few of the words it covers: "a," "cat," "quack," and "Zulu."

For this sequence, a system that knows English assigns a high probability to "quack," since ducks are the animal that quacks. Words like "cat" and "Zulu" receive very low probabilities, since they do not make sense in that position.
The output does not choose a single word directly. It gives a probability for every word in the vocabulary at once, and the most likely words are the ones the system treats as the best completions.

teaching.text: This connects directly to cloze procedure. The system is being asked to fill in a blank at the end of a sequence, and its knowledge of English shows up entirely in how well it completes that blank.

sections.title: Weights carry the system’s learned knowledge

teaching.text: The list of probabilities that GPT produces is called a **pdf,** short for **probability distribution function.** It describes how likely each possible next word is. The input vectors are labeled the **x's,** so the central question is how the system turns the x's into the pdf.
GPT transforms the inputs **through recognizing by computing.** It recognizes the pattern in the input words, and that recognition is carried out entirely through computation.
The computing involved is mostly just **addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division:** +, −, ×, ÷
This is the same **grade school arithmetic** used to add up a grocery bill. The difference is that GPT performs these operations an enormous number of times in a row.
Nothing more mysterious than these four operations is needed to turn a row of word vectors into a list of next-word probabilities.
The **knowledge** the system uses to transform the x's into the pdf is stored **in a bunch of numbers called w's, or weights.**
children: The x's change every time a new sentence comes in, but the w's stay fixed while the system is being used. The arithmetic combines the incoming x's with the stored w's, and the result is the pdf.
The knowledge is located **in** the weights. If the weights are changed, the system's predictions change, which means its knowledge has changed.

teaching.text: Today's AI systems have **about a couple of trillion weights.** Every piece of knowledge the system has, including the fact that ducks quack and chickens cackle, is spread across those trillions of numbers.

sections.title: Weights and synapses as a scale comparison

teaching.text: A couple of trillion weights may seem like far too many numbers for the system to resemble human knowledge. The comparison with the brain points the other way.

A person knows that chickens cackle but ducks quack, and that knowledge has to be stored somewhere. It is stored in the **synapses,** which are the connections between the **neurons** of the brain. A synapse is the point where one neuron passes a signal to another, and the strength of each connection helps determine what the brain does with incoming information.
The human brain has **about 150 trillion synapses.** Comparing this to the roughly 2 trillion weights of an AI system gives: 150 trillion/ 2 trillion = 75
The brain therefore has roughly 75 times as many connections as today's largest AI systems have weights.

In both cases, knowledge is stored in a huge number of connection strengths rather than in a list of written facts. The weights of an AI system play the role that synapses play in the brain, so the number of weights is not unreasonably large when compared to human knowledge.

sections.title: Completion is a form of prediction

teaching.text: The claim that **knowledge is completion** strikes many people as nonsensical. Among them is **Yann LeCun,** a leading AI researcher, who argues that this view does not make sense and just raised **a billion dollars** on the basis of that position.

Anyone who has used an AI system can judge the question directly. The question is whether, while interacting with the system, it feels like a system whose notion of knowledge is **totally different** from our own.
children: One reasonable answer is that whatever the system's notion of knowledge is, it is **not totally different** from ours. Its answers, completions, and explanations are close enough to human knowledge that the two cannot be entirely separate.

teaching.text: Another term for completion is **prediction,** and that word tends to sit better with people. Humans constantly **predict** and **expect** what will happen next, whether it is the next word in a sentence, the next note in a song, or the next event in a situation. Seen this way, knowledge as completion is knowledge as prediction, which is something human minds do all the time.

sections.title: Mistakes provide a direction for learning

teaching.text: One of the most central issues in AI is **how it learns.** AI **learns by making mistakes,** and humans may not be that different.
The cartoon titled "How much you learn," taken from the r/GetMotivated page on Reddit, shows three stacks of books sitting side by side.
children: The stack labeled **"From theory"** is the shortest, with only a few red books.
The stack labeled **"From practice"** is taller, with the red books plus several blue books on top.
The stack labeled **"From mistakes"** is by far the tallest, containing red and blue books topped by a large pile of green books.
The cartoon expresses the idea that people learn the most from their mistakes, which matches the way AI systems learn.

teaching.text: The main algorithm for learning in AI is called **Stochastic Gradient Descent** (SGD). The algorithm can be understood through a very easy example: **averaging.**

sections.title: Averaging as observation-based error learning

teaching.text: Computing an average in the ordinary way is simple. The average of 10, 12, and 14 is found by adding the numbers and dividing by how many there are: (10 + 12 + 14) / 3 = 36 / 3 = 12

This direct method **does not work** for the complex things AI deals with, such as **speech, language, biological molecules, and scenes.** For those, there is no simple formula that can be applied once to get the answer, so a different approach is needed.
The averaging method used in AI works in a way that can be extended to those complex cases.
children: We start with a **list of numbers.**
We make a **wild guess,** called x, about what their average is.
We then **improve x through exposure to the data.** We take one number from the list and compare it to the current value of x. We then move x **a bit closer** to that observed number.
We **repeat** this with another number, and then another.

teaching.text: This is called **observation-based error learning.** The estimate starts out wrong, each observation reveals how wrong it is, and the estimate is corrected a little each time.

sections.title: The correction rule of stochastic gradient descent

teaching.text: The goal is to find the average of the list [78, 67, 98, 85, 76, 68, 98, 72]. The average can be thought of as **the essence** of the list, a single number that best represents all the values in it.
children: For reference, the true average of this list can be computed directly: 78 + 67 + 98 + 85 + 76 + 68 + 98 + 72 = 642 642/8 = 80.25

teaching.text: SGD reaches an estimate close to this value without ever doing that full calculation. It follows these steps:
children: 1. **Pick any random number x as the estimate of the average.** This is **time 0** in the algorithm, so the estimate is written as x[0]. Suppose the random number picked is 130, so x[0] = 130. The guess is deliberately far from the true value, and the algorithm improves it by observation.
2. **Randomly pick a number d from the data.** This shows how far the data is from the estimate, and the average should be close to the data. Suppose the number picked is 98, so d[0] = 98.
3. **Measure the mistake.** The mistake is called the **Loss,** and it is the difference between the current estimate and the observed data point: Loss = x[0] − d[0] = 130 − 98 = 32

teaching.text: 4. **Improve the estimate by subtracting a small part of the Loss from it.** Here that small part is 10% of the Loss: x[1] = x[0] − 10% of 32 10% of 32 = 0.10 × 32 = 3.2 x[1] = 130 − 3.2 = 126.8
5. **Repeat.** Pick another number d from the data and use it in the same way to improve x[1] into x[2], then x[2] into x[3], and so on.

The same rule works when the estimate starts too low. If the estimate were 10 and the data point drawn were 78, the Loss would be 10 minus 78, which is negative 68. Subtracting 10% of a negative number means adding, so the estimate would rise by 6.8, moving from 10 up to 16.8. The estimate is always pushed toward the data, whichever side it starts on.
The whole algorithm does two things. It **makes an initial estimate or guess,** and it **uses data to improve that estimate.**
Each part of the name describes one part of the method.
children: **Stochastic** means **random,** since each data point is picked at random from the list.
**Gradient** refers to the **Loss,** since the size and direction of each correction depend on how large the mistake is and which way it points.
**Descent** means **reducing,** since each step reduces the mistake by moving the estimate closer to the data.

sections.title: Learning rate changes both speed and variability

teaching.text: The fraction of the Loss subtracted at each step is called the **learning rate.** In the example it was 10%. The four graphs show SGD applied to the list above with four different learning rates: 10%, 50%, 1%, **and 80%.**
children: In every graph, the vertical axis is the estimate x, running from 0 to 140, and the horizontal axis is **epochs,** running from 0 to 300. Each epoch here is one update step of the estimate.

Each graph shows three runs that start from three different **initial conditions (IC),** meaning three different starting guesses. The red run starts at **IC = 130,** the green run starts at **IC = 80,** and the blue run starts at IC = 10.

teaching.text: With a learning rate of 10%, the red run drops steeply from 130 and the blue run climbs steeply from 10. Both reach the neighborhood of 80 within roughly the first 25 to 50 epochs. The green run starts near 80 and stays there. After that, all three runs overlap and wobble slightly around 80, staying within a narrow band a few points above and below it.

With a learning rate of 1%, all three runs are **smooth,** with almost no wobble. However, learning is **very slow.** After 300 epochs, the red run has only come down to about 82 and the blue run has only climbed to about 76, so neither has fully reached the average yet. The green run stays flat near 80 the whole time.

With a learning rate of 50%, the red and blue runs jump to the neighborhood of 80 within the first few epochs, so learning is very fast. Afterward, however, all three runs **bounce up and down widely,** roughly between 70 and 95, and never settle on a single value.
With a learning rate of 80%, the runs reach the neighborhood of 80 even faster, but the bouncing is **even larger,** spreading roughly between 65 and 97.

The bouncing comes from the random single data points used at each step. Each update pulls the estimate toward just one number from the list, and those numbers range from 67 to 98. With a small learning rate, each pull moves the estimate only slightly, so the pulls toward high and low values average out. With a large learning rate, each pull moves the estimate most of the way toward whichever number was drawn. At 80%, if the estimate is 80 and the number drawn is 98, the estimate jumps by 80% of the 18-point gap, which is 14.4, landing at 94.4. The next draw may then throw it far back down.

sections.title: The speed–accuracy tradeoff

teaching.text: The four graphs reveal the **fundamental learning tradeoff.** The learning rate is written with the Greek letter γ (gamma).
children: When γ is **increased,** learning **speed increases,** since the estimate reaches the neighborhood of the answer in just a few steps. At the same time, **accuracy decreases,** since the estimate keeps jumping around instead of settling close to the true average.

When γ is **decreased,** learning **speed decreases,** since the estimate creeps toward the answer and may still be far from it after hundreds of steps. At the same time, **accuracy increases,** since the estimate moves smoothly and stays close to the true value once it gets there.

teaching.text: Speed and accuracy pull against each other, so a single learning rate cannot make both as good as possible at once. The 10% learning rate sits between the extremes, reaching the average fairly quickly while wobbling only a little.

For generations, **thousands of people have made their living** by finding better ways to **optimize** learning. Optimizing here means adjusting how learning is carried out so that **speed and accuracy both increase** at the same time, getting around the tradeoff that a single fixed learning rate cannot escape.

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
Elements, relations, and a goal

teaching.text: A **dynamical system** is a system whose state changes over time according to rules. We study dynamical systems in two places: in **animal behavior,** such as an octopus defending its home or a person speaking, and in **AI learning,** where a computer program changes its internal numbers as it is trained.

Every dynamical system can be described with three parts: 1) **Elements, 2) Relations, 3) Goal.** The **elements** are the pieces that make up the system. The **relations** are the ways those pieces are connected and coordinated with each other. The **goal** is what the whole coordinated system is working to achieve.
children: Using these three parts lets us describe very different systems in the same terms, whether the system is an animal's body, a vocal tract, or a machine learning program.

sections.title: An octopus coordinates its body with its environment

teaching.text: An octopus defending its den is a clear example of a dynamical system in behavior. Its **elements** are its 8 **arms** and the **ground** it is sitting on and pushing against.

The **relations** in this system are the coordinated connections between each individual arm, the ground, and the fish the octopus is interacting with. These relations are **planned by a neural system** that lives in the octopus's head and also throughout the rest of its body. The octopus does not control its arms from one central point alone; the planning is spread across the body.
The **goal** of this system is to **keep the den.** The octopus coordinates its arms, its grip on the ground, and the movement of the fish so that it can protect its home.

sections.title: Speech is an organized dynamical system

teaching.text: Human speech is also a dynamical system, and it has many more elements than the octopus example. The **elements** are the **many parts of the tongue,** the **lips,** the **velum,** the **larynx,** the **palate,** and the **pharyngeal wall.**
children: The **tongue** is not one single element; its tip, body, and root can each move somewhat independently, so it counts as many parts.
The **velum** is the soft back part of the roof of the mouth. It raises to close off the nasal passage or lowers to let air flow through the nose.
The **larynx** is the voice box in the throat, which contains the vocal folds that vibrate to produce voicing.
The **palate** is the hard roof of the mouth, and the **pharyngeal wall** is the back wall of the throat behind the tongue.

teaching.text: The **relations** between all these parts are **planned by the brain.** Producing a single word requires the lips, tongue, velum, and larynx to move at precisely coordinated times relative to each other.
The **goal** of the speech system is to **convey a thought.** All of this coordinated movement exists so that an idea in one person's mind can be transmitted to another person.

A **real-time** MRI recording of a speaker shows this system in action. The image is a side view of the head cut down the middle, showing the lips at the front, the tongue filling the mouth, the palate and velum above the tongue, and the throat and spine running down the back. Over about three seconds of speech, the lips, jaw, and tongue change shape and position continuously, which shows that speech is a set of many parts moving together over time rather than a series of frozen positions.

sections.title: Shared organization across very different systems

teaching.text: All of our **daily voluntary actions,** such as walking or reaching, are dynamical systems. The **involuntary actions** of the **heart,** the **pancreas,** and **neurons** are dynamical systems too, since each involves parts whose activity changes over time in coordinated ways.

The elements of a dynamical system can be very large or very small. They can be as big as **organs** or parts of organs, and as small as **cells** and the **chemicals** inside cells. **Biology, chemistry, and physics** are all fields that study dynamical systems at these different scales.
The **speech system** is a **very complex dynamical system,** since it combines many body parts, many muscles, and brain planning all working toward one goal.

There are so many dynamical systems in nature that we can **use one dynamical system to study another.** Two systems can be extremely different on the surface, such as an octopus arm and a human tongue, while still sharing an **underlying similarity** in how their elements, relations, and goals are organized.
children: This idea is described as **going up Diotima's ladder.** Diotima is a figure in Plato's Symposium who describes rising from appreciating particular individual examples to understanding the general form they all share. Studying many different dynamical systems moves us from individual cases toward the general principles that all of them have in common.

sections.title: Motor primitives combine into a complex octopus action

teaching.text: The octopus example comes from a published study: **"A syntactic analysis of a complex motor action: the octopus arm 'slap'"** by **Jean Alupay, Jennifer Mather, and Khalil Iskarous,** published in **Marine Biology in 2023.** The paper was received on 15 February 2023 and accepted on 1 June 2023.

The researchers studied an octopus of the genus **Abdopus,** filmed in **tidal pools in Okinawa, Japan,** as it **"slapped" at fish** in the wild. A **slap** is a quick arm strike the octopus uses against a fish near its den.
children: In total, 19 **slaps were analyzed.**

The arm movements were measured in two **reference frames.** An **external reference frame** measures position relative to the surrounding environment, and an **animal-centered reference frame** measures position relative to the octopus's own body.

teaching.text: The octopus built each slap out of two **kinematic primitives,** which are basic building- block movements. These two primitives are **rotation** and **translation** of its **hydrostatic arms.** Rotation means turning the arm around a point, and translation means moving the arm from one place to another without turning it.
children: A **muscular hydrostat** is a body structure with no bones that is supported by muscles pushing against each other around an incompressible core. The octopus arm is a muscular hydrostat, which is why it can bend at any point along its length.
The octopus combined these primitives **serially,** meaning one after another, and **in parallel,** meaning at the same time.

teaching.text: By combining a small number of primitives, the octopus keeps its movement **flexible** while only having to control **a few degrees of freedom.** A **degree of freedom** is one independent way a system can move. An octopus arm could in principle bend in almost unlimited ways, so limiting control to a few combined primitives makes the movement manageable. The authors named this concept **flexible rigidity.**

The slap supports **Flash and Hochner's embodied organization** view of motor behavior. This view holds that much of the organization of movement comes from the structure of the body itself, not only from commands in the brain. It also supports their idea that **motor primitives can combine syntactically** to form a complex action.
children: **Syntax** in language is the set of rules for combining words into larger structures like sentences. Calling the slap **syntactic** means that small movement units are combined by rules into a larger action, in the same way words are combined into sentences. This is a direct case of using one dynamical system, the octopus arm, to study another, human language.

teaching.text: The octopus uses **sensory feedback** about the position of the moving fish together with **feed-forward** motor primitives. **Feedback** is information coming in from the senses during the movement that allows correction. **Feed-forward** control means sending out a pre-planned movement without waiting for correction. Combining the two lets the octopus build complex actions that stay in **dynamic equilibrium** with the environment, meaning the octopus keeps adjusting so that its actions remain balanced with a changing situation.

These findings give a more realistic picture of how a complex behavior allows an animal to **coordinate with its environment.** The paper's keywords are **Octopus, Muscular hydrostat, Motor control,** and **Abdopus.**

The book **Octopus: The Ocean's Intelligent Invertebrate — A Natural History** by **Jennifer A. Mather, Roland** C. **Anderson, and James** B. **Wood** is a broader source on octopus behavior and intelligence. Jennifer Mather is also a co-author of the slap study.

sections.title: Knowledge and other psychological skills in AI

teaching.text: **AI** is a **model of several animal psychological skills.** It is a system built to imitate abilities that animals, including humans, already have. The five skills are **knowing, recognizing, attending, acting,** and **learning.**
children: **Knowing** is holding stored information about the world, such as information about how words are used.
**Recognizing** is identifying what something is when it is encountered, such as recognizing a word or a face.
**Attending** is focusing on the parts of the input that matter most at a given moment.
**Acting** is producing an output, such as a movement for an animal or a word for a language model.
**Learning** is changing internal knowledge based on experience so that future performance improves.

teaching.text: The **Cloze Procedure** is an early example of measuring one of these skills in humans. It was introduced by **Wilson** L. **Taylor** in **"'Cloze Procedure': A New Tool for Measuring Readability,"** published in **Journalism Quarterly** in **Fall 1953.**
children: In a **cloze task,** words are removed from a passage and readers must fill in the blanks. The more easily readers can guess the missing words, the more readable and predictable the text is.

Taylor's article was the first full statement of the method and its theory, which had first been introduced briefly at a workshop at the 1953 **AEJ convention.** It included findings from **three pilot studies** and **two experiments** comparing cloze results with those of **two readability formulas.**
Filling in a missing word from its context is the same basic skill that modern language AI is built to perform: predicting a word from the words around it.

sections.title: Inputs, knowledge, and a predicted distribution

teaching.text: In GPT, each word is represented as a **vector,** which is a list of **thousands of numbers.** We call these vectors **x's** or **tokens.** In the example sentence **"chickens cackle and ducks,"** each of the four words is its own tall column of numbers, one column for each token.

All of the AI's **knowledge** about speech, language, or anything else is stored in **a few trillion numbers** called **weights,** or **w's.** The weights are not a dictionary or a list of facts; they are numbers whose values together determine how the system responds to input.

The AI combines its knowledge, the **W's,** with the input vectors, the **x's,** using mostly the four basic operations: **addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (+ ,−,× ,÷).** The complexity of the system comes from the enormous number of these simple calculations, not from any complicated single operation.

These calculations produce a **probability distribution function** over possible next words. A **probability distribution** assigns each possible word a probability, and all the probabilities together add up to one. This distribution is the system's way of saying, "this is my guess for the next word."
children: Given "chickens cackle and ducks," the distribution is spread across a line of possible words that includes **"a," "cat," "quack,"** and **"Zulu."** The curve over this line has small bumps over many words, showing that many words get a little probability, and a tallest peak over **"quack,"** showing that "quack" is the system's most likely guess.

teaching.text: The way the **W's combine with the X's** to produce this prediction is itself a **dynamical system. Learning** is a simpler dynamical system than this prediction process, which makes it the easier one to work through first.

sections.title: How initially random weights become useful

teaching.text: The weights, which hold all of the system's knowledge, come from a training process that starts with no knowledge at all. The approach is summed up as **"Fake it till you make it!"**
Training follows a repeated sequence of steps:
children: 1. The system **starts with random W's.** These are completely random numbers, and any values at all can be used as the starting point.
2. The system is given a sequence of words, such as **"chickens cackle and ducks,"** and is asked to **predict the next word** by combining its W's with the input vectors.

3. With random weights, the prediction is poor. The system's distribution might have its tallest peak over **"cat,"** with only low, uneven probability spread across the other words, including "quack."

4. We already know the correct next word is **"quack."** The **target distribution** puts all of the probability on "quack" as a single sharp spike and zero probability on every other word. We tell the system to **change its W's** so that its output distribution looks more like this target.
5. The system is exposed to **more sequences** and asked to predict the next word again, **billions of times,** and each time its W's are changed to **improve its guessing.**

teaching.text: This repeated cycle of guessing, comparing to the correct answer, and adjusting the weights is **how** LLMs **learn and know.** An LLM, or **large language model,** gets all of its knowledge from this process of gradually correcting random weights over billions of examples.

sections.title: Random initialization and learning from mistakes

teaching.text: AI learning depends on **two tricks,** each captured by a phrase in an image generated by **ChatGPT.**

The first trick is **"Fake It Till You Make It."** The system begins with **random weights** and makes predictions right away, even though those first predictions are essentially meaningless. It does not wait until it has knowledge before acting; it acts first and gains knowledge along the way.

The second trick is **"Learn by Making Mistakes."** Each wrong prediction produces an **error,** which is the difference between what the system guessed and what was correct. The system uses that error to adjust its weights, so every mistake becomes information that improves the next prediction.

sections.title: A simple model of learning an average

teaching.text: Finding an **average** seems very easy when we have a short list of numbers. The average of 10, 12, and 14 is found by adding the numbers and dividing by how many there are: (10 + 12 + 14) / 3 = 12

This simple formula **does not work for more complex things** like **speech, language, biological molecules, and scenes,** which are exactly the kinds of things AI works with. For those, there is no short list of numbers we can simply add up and divide, so we need a method that improves an estimate step by step instead.
The averaging method used here works by **learning from the data one piece at a time:**
children: We start with a **list of numbers.**
We make a **wild guess,** called x, about what their average is.
We improve x through **exposure to the data.** We take one number from the list and examine it with respect to the current value of x, checking how far apart they are.

We then improve x by moving it **a bit closer** to the number we observed from the data. This is called **observation-based error learning,** since each observation reveals an error in the current guess and the guess is corrected in the direction of that observation.
We **repeat** this with another number, and then another, so that the guess keeps being corrected.

teaching.text: This is the same logic as training an LLM, applied to a much simpler problem. The random starting guess for x plays the role of the random starting weights, and moving x toward each observed number plays the role of changing the weights toward the correct next word.

sections.title: Start from an arbitrary estimate

teaching.text: SGD, or **stochastic gradient descent,** is the learning method that estimates an average by learning from the data one observation at a time. The question it answers is: what is the average, the **essence,** of this list of numbers? [78, 67, 98, 85, 76, 68, 98, 72]

The true average of this list is found by adding the eight numbers and dividing by eight. This value serves as the target that the learning process should approach. (78 + 67 + 98 + 85 + 76 + 68 + 98 + 72) / 8 = 642 / 8 = 80.25

SGD does not start by calculating this average. It starts by picking **any random number x** as the estimate. At **time 0,** the starting estimate is set to 130, which is far above every number in the list. x[0] = 130
The number in brackets is the **time step,** so x[0] is the estimate at time 0, x[1] is the estimate after one update, and so on.
The **learning rate,** written γ, is set to 25%. The learning rate controls how large each correction is, meaning what fraction of the error the estimate moves on each step. γ = 25% = 0.25
Plotted against the update number, the estimate at time 0 is a single point at 130, while the true average of 80.25 sits far below it as a flat horizontal line.

sections.title: An observation exposes a discrepancy

teaching.text: The first step of learning is to **randomly pick one number d** from the data. The first observation drawn is 98. d[0] = 98

The current estimate is x[0] = 130. The **discrepancy,** also called the **loss,** is the difference between the current estimate and the observation. The loss measures how wrong the estimate is compared to this piece of data. 130 − 98 = 32

The discrepancy is positive, which means the estimate is 32 units too high compared to this observation. The average of a data set should be **close to the data,** so an estimate that is far from an observed value is a sign that the estimate needs to change.
Plotted together at update 0, the estimate is at 130 and the observation is at 98, below it, with the true average of 80.25 lower still.

sections.title: Correct a fraction rather than replacing the guess

teaching.text: The correction step **subtracts 25% of the discrepancy** from the current estimate. With a discrepancy of 32 and a learning rate of 0.25, the size of the correction is found first. 0.25 × 32 = 8
That correction is subtracted from the current estimate to give the new estimate. x[1] = 130 − 0.25(32) x[1] = 130 − 8 = 122

The estimate moves **toward this observation.** It does not jump all the way to 98; it only moves one quarter of the distance, from 130 to 122. Moving only part of the way keeps any single observation from taking over the estimate.
Plotted over updates, the estimate line drops from 130 at update 0 to 122 at update 1, heading down toward the average line at 80.25.

sections.title: Correction after observation 2

teaching.text: The same procedure is repeated with a new random observation each time: draw a number, compute the discrepancy, and subtract 25% of that discrepancy from the estimate.
On the second update, the random observation is 85. The discrepancy between the current estimate of 122 and this observation is computed first. d[1] = 85 122 − 85 = 37
The correction is 25% of 37, and subtracting it gives the new estimate. 0.25 × 37 = 9.25 x[2] = 122 − 0.25(37) = 122 − 9.25 = 112.75
The estimate moves toward this observation, dropping from 122 to 112.75.

sections.title: Correction after observation 3

teaching.text: On the third update, the random observation is 76. The discrepancy is again positive, since the estimate is still above the observation. d[2] = 76 112.75 − 76 = 36.75
The correction is 25% of 36.75, which is then subtracted from the estimate. 0.25 × 36.75 = 9.1875 x[3] = 112.75 − 0.25(36.75) = 112.75 − 9.1875 ≈ 103.563
The estimate moves toward this observation, dropping from 112.75 to about 103.563.

sections.title: Correction after observation 4

teaching.text: On the fourth update, the random observation is 68. d[3] = 68 103.563 − 68 = 35.563
The correction is 25% of 35.563, which is subtracted from the estimate. 0.25 × 35.563 ≈ 8.891 x[4] = 103.563 − 0.25(35.563) = 103.563 − 8.891 = 94.672
The estimate moves toward this observation, dropping from 103.563 to 94.672.

Across the first four updates, the estimate falls steadily: 130, 122, 112.75, 103.563, and 94.672. Every observation so far has been below the estimate, so every correction has pushed the estimate down toward the average line at 80.25.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: On the fifth update, the random observation is 98, which is **higher** than the current estimate of 94.672. A **datum** is a single data point. d[4] = 98
The discrepancy is now **negative,** since the estimate is below the observation. 94.672 − 98 = −3.328
The rule still says to subtract 25% of the discrepancy. The correction is a negative number. 0.25 × (−3.328) = −0.832 x[5] = 94.672 − 0.25(−3.328) = 94.672 + 0.832 = 95.504

**Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding,** so a negative discrepancy makes the subtraction **move x upward.** The estimate rises slightly from 94.672 to 95.504, toward the high observation.
children: The same single rule handles both cases. When the estimate is above an observation, the discrepancy is positive and the estimate goes down; when the estimate is below an observation, the discrepancy is negative and the estimate goes up. In both cases the estimate moves toward the observation.

teaching.text: Plotted over updates, the estimate line bends slightly upward at update 5 after four straight drops, which is the first sign that the path does not move smoothly in one direction.

sections.title: Correction after observation 6

teaching.text: On the sixth update, the random observation is 72, which is below the estimate again. d[5] = 72 95.504 − 72 = 23.504
The correction is 25% of 23.504, which is subtracted from the estimate. 0.25 × 23.504 = 5.876 x[6] = 95.504 − 0.25(23.504) = 95.504 − 5.876 = 89.628
The estimate moves toward this observation, dropping from 95.504 to 89.628.

sections.title: Correction after observation 7

teaching.text: On the seventh update, the random observation is 78. d[6] = 78 89.628 − 78 = 11.628

The discrepancy is smaller than before, since the estimate is now much closer to the data. The correction is 25% of 11.628. 0.25 × 11.628 = 2.907 x[7] = 89.628 − 0.25(11.628) = 89.628 − 2.907 = 86.721
The estimate moves toward this observation, dropping from 89.628 to 86.721.

sections.title: Correction after observation 8

teaching.text: On the eighth update, the random observation is 67, the lowest number in the list. d[7] = 67 86.721 − 67 = 19.721
The correction is 25% of 19.721, which is subtracted from the estimate. 0.25 × 19.721 ≈ 4.930 x[8] = 86.721 − 0.25(19.721) = 86.721 − 4.930 = 81.791
The estimate moves toward this observation, dropping from 86.721 to 81.791. After eight updates, the estimate is only about 1.5 above the true average of 80.25.

sections.title: A high observation pulls the estimate upward

teaching.text: On the ninth update, the random observation is 98 once more. The value 98 appears twice in the list, and since each draw is random, the same value can be picked more than once. This is the third time 98 has been drawn. d[8] = 98
The estimate of 81.791 is well below 98, so the discrepancy is negative and fairly large. 81.791 − 98 = −16.209
Subtracting 25% of a negative discrepancy moves the estimate upward. 0.25 × (−16.209) ≈ −4.052 x[9] = 81.791 − 0.25(−16.209) = 81.791 + 4.052 = 85.843

A negative discrepancy makes the subtraction move x upward, from 81.791 to 85.843. A single high observation pushed the estimate away from the true average, even though the estimate had been getting very close. This shows that each step responds only to the one observation drawn, not to the whole data set.

sections.title: Correction after observation 10

teaching.text: On the tenth update, the random observation is 85, which is extremely close to the current estimate. d[9] = 85 85.843 − 85 = 0.843
The discrepancy is less than 1, so the correction is tiny. 0.25 × 0.843 ≈ 0.211 x[10] = 85.843 − 0.25(0.843) = 85.843 − 0.211 = 85.632
The estimate barely moves, from 85.843 to 85.632. When an observation agrees closely with the estimate, the estimate hardly changes.

sections.title: Correction after observation 11

teaching.text: On the eleventh update, the random observation is 76. d[10] = 76 85.632 − 76 = 9.632
The correction is 25% of 9.632, which is subtracted from the estimate. 0.25 × 9.632 = 2.408 x[11] = 85.632 − 0.25(9.632) = 85.632 − 2.408 = 83.224
The estimate moves toward this observation, dropping from 85.632 to 83.224.

sections.title: Correction after observation 12

teaching.text: On the twelfth update, the random observation is 68. d[11] = 68 83.224 − 68 = 15.224
The correction is 25% of 15.224, which is subtracted from the estimate. 0.25 × 15.224 = 3.806 x[12] = 83.224 − 0.25(15.224) = 83.224 − 3.806 = 79.418
The estimate moves toward this observation, dropping from 83.224 to 79.418. This is less than 1 below the true average of 80.25, even though the process started at 130.

Over all twelve updates, the estimate went 130, 122, 112.75, 103.563, 94.672, 95.504, 89.628, 86.721, 81.791, 85.843, 85.632, 83.224, and 79.418. The path falls steeply at first, bumps upward twice when 98 is drawn, and ends up hovering near the average line.

sections.title: Why the learning path jitters
