teaching.text: SGD consists of two steps. First, **make an initial estimate or guess,** which can be completely random. Second, **use data to improve the estimate,** one observation at a time, by moving the estimate part of the way toward each observation.
Each word in the name describes part of the method.
children: **Stochastic** means **random observation.** At each step, the data point used for the correction is picked at random from the data set, which is why the estimate is sometimes pushed down and sometimes pulled up.

**Gradient** means a **loss-related direction.** The discrepancy tells us both how wrong the estimate is and which direction it needs to move: a positive discrepancy means move down, and a negative discrepancy means move up.
**Descent** means **reducing the mistake.** Every correction is chosen so that the error for the observed data point gets smaller.

teaching.text: **The path jitters, but its tendency is toward the average.** Individual steps can move away from the true average, as happened when 98 was drawn, but over many updates the random pushes up and down balance out and the estimate settles near about 80, the average of the data.
This is observation-based error learning in its simplest form. The same method, applied to trillions of weights instead of a single number x, is how LLMs change their W's to predict the next word.

sections.title: An estimate can fall while its loss falls

teaching.text: A **second data set** makes the relationship between the estimate and the loss easier to track. [62, 70, 78, 82, 90, 98]
The average of this data set is 80. (62 + 70 + 78 + 82 + 90 + 98) / 6 = 480 / 6 = 80

The **mean motion of** SGD describes how the estimate moves on average. Each random observation is sometimes above and sometimes below the average, so on average the estimate is pulled toward the mean of the data, 80. Replacing the random observation with the average gives the rule for the mean motion. x[t + 1] = x[t] − 0.25 (x[t] − 80)
Here t stands for any time step, so this one equation describes every update. The new estimate x[t + 1] equals the old estimate x[t] minus 25% of the distance between the old estimate and 80.
The **loss** at each time step is defined as one half of the discrepancy squared. L[t] = 1/2 (x[t] − 80)²
**Squaring** the discrepancy makes the loss positive whether the estimate is too high or too low, so both kinds of mistakes count as error. The loss is zero only when the estimate equals 80 exactly.

The rate at which this loss changes as x changes is equal to the discrepancy x[t] − 80. This is why the discrepancy is the **gradient,** the loss-related direction, and why subtracting a fraction of it moves the estimate in the direction that lowers the loss.
The starting point is set far above the average. x[0] = 140
At time 0, the loss is computed from the discrepancy of 60. L[0] = 1/2 (140 − 80)² = 1/2 (60)² = 1/2 (3600) = 1800

Each update keeps 75% of the previous discrepancy, so the discrepancy shrinks from 60 to 45 to 33.75 and continues shrinking. The estimate curve falls quickly at first and then flattens out as it approaches the target line at 80, reaching about 82 by update 12. The loss curve falls from 1800 at update 0 to nearly 0 by update 12.

Unlike the stochastic path, the mean motion is **smooth** with no jitter, since it uses the average of the data instead of a random observation at each step. In this case, the **estimate goes down and the loss goes down** together.

sections.title: An estimate can rise while its loss falls

teaching.text: The same data set and the same learning rate, γ = 25%, can be used with only the **initial condition** changed. The **initial condition** is the starting value of the estimate. This time the estimate starts far below the average. x[0] = −100
At time 0, the discrepancy is negative, but squaring makes the loss positive and very large. L[0] = 1/2 (−100 − 80)² = 1/2 (−180)² = 1/2 (32400) = 16200

On the first update, subtracting 25% of a negative discrepancy moves the estimate upward. x[1] = −100 − 0.25(−100 − 80) = −100 − 0.25(−180) = −100 + 45 = −55 L[1] = 1/2 (−55 − 80)² = 1/2 (−135)² = 1/2 (18225) = 9112.5

**The estimate rises toward 80,** climbing from −100 to about 74 by update 12. **The discrepancy shrinks** in size at every step, and so **one half of the discrepancy squared falls toward 0,** dropping from 16,200 at update 0 to nearly 0 by update 12.

**The direction changes, but the learning does not.** Starting above the average, the estimate moves down; starting below the average, the estimate moves up. In both cases the loss decreases, which means that learning is defined by the loss going down, not by the estimate moving in any particular direction.

sections.title: Learning rate and starting condition

teaching.text: SGD can be run for 300 **epochs,** meaning 300 update steps, with three different initial conditions and four different learning rates. The three initial conditions are **IC = 130,** which starts well above the average; **IC = 80,** which starts right at the average; and **IC =** 10, which starts well below it. Every run settles around 80, the average of the data.

With a **learning rate of 10%,** the run starting at 130 falls and the run starting at 10 rises, and both reach the neighborhood of 80 within about the first 25 to 50 epochs. After that, all three runs wiggle gently within a few units of 80, roughly between 75 and 85. The run starting at 80 stays near 80 throughout, with only small jitters.

With a **learning rate of 50%,** the runs starting at 130 and at 10 reach the neighborhood of 80 within the first few epochs. After that, however, all three runs jump up and down widely, roughly between 70 and 95, and never settle down.

With a **learning rate of 1%,** the runs move very slowly and very smoothly. After 300 epochs, the run starting at 130 has only come down to about 82, and the run starting at 10 has only climbed to about 77, so neither has fully reached the average. The run starting at 80 stays almost perfectly flat at 80 with very little jitter.

With a **learning rate of 80%,** the runs starting at 130 and at 10 reach the average region almost immediately. After that, all three runs jump violently, roughly between 68 and 98, which is nearly the full range of the data values. With such a high learning rate, each update moves the estimate most of the way to whatever observation was just drawn, so the estimate mostly tracks individual data points instead of their average.

The initial condition affects only the first part of each run. After enough epochs, all three runs behave the same way, and the size of the learning rate determines how fast they arrive and how much they jitter once they get there.

sections.title: The learning tradeoff

teaching.text: The learning rate creates a **fundamental learning tradeoff** between speed and accuracy.
children: When γ **increases,** learning **speed increases,** since each correction is larger and the estimate reaches the average region in fewer steps. At the same time, **accuracy decreases,** since the large corrections make the estimate jump around the average instead of settling on it.

When γ **decreases,** learning **speed decreases,** since each correction is small and the estimate needs many steps to reach the average. At the same time, **accuracy increases,** since the small corrections keep the estimate steady and close to the true average once it arrives.

teaching.text: This tradeoff is an unhappy fact of learning: with a single learning rate, we cannot have the fastest learning and the most accurate result at the same time. The 1% run is accurate but slow, and the 50% and 80% runs are fast but noisy.

**Thousands of people, for generations, have made their living** finding better ways to **optimize,** meaning to adjust a learning process so that it works as well as possible. The goal of this work is to find methods where **speed increases and accuracy increases** together, so that systems like LLMs can learn quickly while still ending up with accurate weights.

lecture04.title: 04 · Dynamic programming and shared physical principles

sections.title: Dynamical systems 1
Lecture agenda
A staged shortest-path problem

teaching.text: The **shortest path problem** asks for the cheapest route through a network of connected points, from a starting point to an ending point. Each point is a **state,** which is a place we can be at a given moment. Each arrow is a possible move from one state to another, and each arrow has a number attached to it called its **cost.** The cost can stand for distance, time, effort, or anything we want to keep as small as possible. The total cost of a route is the sum of the costs on every arrow along it, and the goal is to find the route whose total is smallest.

In our network, we start at **A** and want to reach **J.** The states are arranged in columns called **stages,** and every arrow moves us forward exactly one stage. We can never skip a stage or move backward.
children: Stage one contains only A. Stage two contains B and C. Stage three contains D, E, and F. Stage four contains G, H, and I. Stage five contains only J, the goal.
Any route from A to J therefore crosses exactly four arrows and makes exactly four decisions, one at each stage.

teaching.text: The costs out of A and out of the second stage are the first ones we face.
children: From A, the arrow to B costs 12 and the arrow to C costs 7.
From B, the arrow to D costs 5, the arrow to E costs 6, and the arrow to F costs 9.
From C, the arrow to D costs 14, the arrow to E costs 10, and the arrow to F costs 11.

teaching.text: The costs out of the third stage lead into the fourth stage.
children: From D, the arrow to G costs 8, the arrow to H costs 7, and the arrow to I costs 10.
From E, the arrow to G costs 9, the arrow to H costs 7, and the arrow to I costs 9.
From F, the arrow to G costs 10, the arrow to H costs 7, and the arrow to I costs 8.

teaching.text: The fourth stage has only one arrow out of each state, and each of those arrows goes to J.
children: From G to J costs 5, from H to J costs 9, and from I to J costs 8.

teaching.text: This network is a model of **decision-making over time.** Every choice has an immediate cost, and every choice also controls which states, and therefore which future costs, are available at the next stage. A choice that looks good now can lock us into expensive moves later.

sections.title: Why the locally cheapest choice can lose

teaching.text: A **greedy algorithm** makes each decision by looking only at the arrows leaving the current state and taking the cheapest one. It never looks further ahead than one move. At every state it asks only which next step is cheapest right now.
Following the greedy rule from A through the network produces one specific route.
children: At A, the choices are 12 to B and 7 to C. The cheaper move is 7, so greed takes us to **C.**
At C, the choices are 14 to D, 10 to E, and 11 to F. The cheapest move is 10, so greed takes us to **E.**
At E, the choices are 9 to G, 7 to H, and 9 to I. The cheapest move is 7, so greed takes us to **H.**
At H, there is only one arrow, which goes to J and costs 9, so we are forced to take it.

teaching.text: The total cost of the greedy route A, C, E, H, J is: 7 + 10 + 7 + 9 = 33
This is not the best we can do. The route A, B, D, G, J starts with the more expensive first move of 12, but its total cost is smaller: 12 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 30

**Greed is not good** for this problem. The greedy rule failed at the very first decision, since the cheap move to C led into a part of the network where every continuation was more costly. Greed also walked right into H, which ends with the large final cost of 9. The greedy algorithm has no way of knowing about costs that come later, so a late obstacle can make an early cheap-looking choice a bad one.
A very small network makes the failure of greed easy to see. From a starting state there are two routes to an ending state, and each route passes through one middle state.
children: On the top route, the first arrow costs 10 and the second arrow, from the top middle state to the end, also costs 10.
On the bottom route, the first arrow costs only 2, but the second arrow, from the bottom middle state to the end, costs 100.

teaching.text: A greedy decision at the start compares 10 with 2 and picks the bottom route. It then gets stuck paying 100 on the next move. The two totals are: 10 + 10 = 20 and 2 + 100 = 102
The top route is five times cheaper than the greedy one, even though its first step was five times more expensive.

Written inside each middle state is the cost of getting from that state to the end: 10 inside the top middle state and 100 inside the bottom middle state. Once each middle state carries this number, the decision at the start becomes simple. We add the cost of the first arrow to the number stored in the state it leads to, and compare 20 with 102. Storing the cost of the rest of the journey inside each state removes the blindness of greed.

sections.title: Blank source page
Exhaustive search trades speed for certainty

teaching.text: An **exhaustive algorithm** solves the shortest path problem by brute force. It lists every possible route from start to end, adds up the cost of each one, and picks the route with the smallest total. Nothing is skipped, so the answer is **guaranteed to be correct.** The method is very accurate.
In our network, the number of routes comes from multiplying the number of choices at each stage.
children: From A there are 2 choices, from the second stage there are 3 choices, and from the third stage there are 3 choices. From the fourth stage there is only 1 choice, since every state there goes straight to J.
The number of complete routes is: 2 × 3 × 3 × 1 = 18

teaching.text: Each of these 18 routes crosses 4 arrows, so each one needs 3 additions to get its total. Checking every route takes 54 additions, followed by comparing 18 totals to find the smallest.

The problem with exhaustive search is its growth. Every added stage multiplies the number of routes by the number of choices at that stage, and every added state per stage makes each of those multipliers larger. If there are **many stages and many states,** the number of routes explodes, and checking all of them takes a very, very long time. Exhaustive search is accurate but becomes impractical for large problems, while greedy search is fast but can be wrong. We need a method that is both accurate and effciient.

sections.title: Bellman’s decomposition

teaching.text: **Bellman** approached the problem by starting with an imaginary step. Imagine we already knew the best possible cost of getting from B to J, and the best possible cost of getting from C to J. We call these numbers VBJ and VCJ. The letter V stands for **Value,** and the Value of a state is the lowest total cost of getting from that state to the goal.
If those two Values were known, the best cost from A to J, which is VAJ, would follow from one short calculation.
children: Any route out of A must go first to either B or C, since those are the only two arrows leaving A.
If we go to B, we pay 12 for that arrow, and then the best we can possibly do for the rest of the trip is V BJ . So the best total through B is 12 + V BJ .
If we go to C, we pay 7 for that arrow, and then the best we can do for the rest of the trip is V CJ . So the best total through C is 7 + V CJ .
The best cost from A is whichever of these two totals is smaller. This is written as: V_AJ = min{12 + V_BJ, 7 + V_CJ}

teaching.text: The word **min** means we take the minimum, which is the smallest number in the set inside the braces. Each number in the set is built the same way. It is the cost of one arrow plus the Value of the state that arrow leads to.

sections.title: Solve the smaller problems that supply the values

teaching.text: The diffciulty is that we **don't know VBJ** or VCJ. The equation for VAJ is correct, but it depends on two numbers we have not yet found.

Bellman's general strategy handles exactly this situation. **To solve a problem, decompose it into subproblems you can solve.** The finding of VAJ becomes two smaller problems, finding VBJ and finding VCJ. The phrase "if you can" matters here. If a subproblem still cannot be solved directly, it gets broken down again into even smaller subproblems.

sections.title: Propagating known costs backward

teaching.text: Bellman's reasoning at A applies in the same way at B. We don't know the best cost from B to J, but if we knew the best costs from D, E, and F to J, then we could find the best cost from B to J.
children: From B we can go to D for 5, to E for 6, or to F for 9. After each move, the best we can do is the Value of the state we arrived at. The best cost from B is the smallest of the three totals: V_BJ = min{5 + V_DJ, 6 + V_EJ, 9 + V_FJ}

teaching.text: C works the same way, with the arrows to D costing 14, to E costing 10, and to F costing 11: V_CJ = min{14 + V_DJ, 10 + V_EJ, 11 + V_FJ}
These equations still depend on unknown Values, so the decomposition continues one more stage. The Values of D, E, and F depend on the Values of G, H, and I.
children: From D, the arrows cost 8 to G, 7 to H, and 10 to I: V_DJ = min{8 + V_GJ, 7 + V_HJ, 10 + V_IJ}

teaching.text: From E, the arrows cost 9 to G, 7 to H, and 9 to I: V_EJ = min{9 + V_GJ, 7 + V_HJ, 9 + V_IJ}
From F, the arrows cost 10 to G, 7 to H, and 8 to I: V_FJ = min{10 + V_GJ, 7 + V_HJ, 8 + V_IJ}

At the fourth stage, the subproblems finally become ones we can solve directly. Each of G, H, and I has exactly one arrow, and it goes straight to J. There is no decision to make, so each Value is simply the cost of that single arrow: V_GJ = 5, V_HJ = 9, V_IJ = 8

The equations form a chain of dependence that runs from the end of the network back to the start. The known Values of G, H, and I feed into the equations for D, E, and F. Once D, E, and F are known, their Values feed into the equations for B and C. Once B and C are known, their Values feed into the single equation for A. Information about the cost of reaching J travels **backward** through the network, one stage at a time, starting from the states closest to the goal.

sections.title: Choose the best total after calculating values

teaching.text: With the Values of G, H, and I known, the Values of the third stage can be calculated directly by substituting V GJ = 5 ,V HJ = 9, and V IJ = 8 into each equation.
children: For D, the three totals are 8 plus 5, 7 plus 9, and 10 plus 8: V_DJ = min{8 + 5, 7 + 9, 10 + 8} = min{13, 16, 18} = 13

teaching.text: For E, the three totals are 9 plus 5, 7 plus 9, and 9 plus 8: V_EJ = min{9 + 5, 7 + 9, 9 + 8} = min{14, 16, 17} = 14
For F, the three totals are 10 plus 5, 7 plus 9, and 8 plus 8: V_FJ = min{10 + 5, 7 + 9, 8 + 8} = min{15, 16, 16} = 15
In all three cases the smallest total comes from going to G. G has the smallest Value of the fourth stage, 5, and that outweighs the differences in the arrow costs.
The third-stage Values, V DJ = 13 ,V EJ = 14, and V FJ = 15, now go into the equations for B and C.
children: For B, the totals are 5 plus 13, 6 plus 14, and 9 plus 15: V_BJ = min{5 + 13, 6 + 14, 9 + 15} = min{18, 20, 24} = 18

teaching.text: For C, the totals are 14 plus 13, 10 plus 14, and 11 plus 15: V_CJ = min{14 + 13, 10 + 14, 11 + 15} = min{27, 24, 26} = 24
Finally, V BJ = 18 and V CJ = 24 go into the equation for A: V_AJ = min{12 + 18, 7 + 24} = min{30, 31} = 30
The best possible cost from A to J is 30. Every state in the network now carries its Value: A is 30, B is 18, C is 24, D is 13, E is 14, F is 15, G is 5, H is 9, and I is 8.

The best path comes from **going greedy on the Values, not on the costs.** At each state, we compare the options by adding the cost of the arrow to the Value of the state it leads to, and we take the smallest sum. This is still a one-step-at-a-time choice, just like the greedy algorithm, but now each option already includes the whole future.
children: At A, going to B gives 12 plus 18, which is 30, and going to C gives 7 plus 24, which is 31. We go to **B,** even though its arrow is the more expensive one.
At B, going to D gives 5 plus 13, which is 18, going to E gives 6 plus 14, which is 20, and going to F gives 9 plus 15, which is 24. We go to **D.**
At D, going to G gives 8 plus 5, which is 13, going to H gives 7 plus 9, which is 16, and going to I gives 10 plus 8, which is 18. We go to **G.**
From G, the only move is to J.

teaching.text: The best path is **A, B, D, G, J,** and its total is 12 plus 5 plus 8 plus 5, which equals 30. This matches VAJ exactly.

**Dynamic programming** is this two-part method. First, calculate the Values by working backward from the goal. Second, choose moves greedily using those Values. The method needed only one small minimum calculation per state instead of adding up all 18 routes one by one.

sections.title: A value summarizes the relevant future

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming is foresight.** Consider standing at the third stage, at D, E, or F. Greedy reasoning based only on arrow costs would often be pulled toward H, since the arrow into H costs 7 from every one of D, E, and F, which is the cheapest or tied for cheapest at each of them. Dynamic programming reveals that **state H leads to something terrible:** the arrow out of H into J costs 9, the largest final cost in the network, so H has the largest Value in its stage.
children: At E, for example, the arrow cost alone favors H at 7 over G at 9. Adding the Values changes the answer. Going to H gives 7 plus 9, which is 16, while going to G gives 9 plus 5, which is 14. The Value of H warns us about the 9 before we ever reach it.

teaching.text: This warning still works if there are many more stages between the current state and J. However far away the bad cost lies, it has already been folded into the Values of every state that leads toward it.

In the original problem, a **late obstacle,** the 9 on the arrow from H to J, caused an early greedy decision based on arrow cost to lead to a bad path. The greedy algorithm picked C at the first step and ended up paying for that 9 at the last step.

**The Values contain the future.** Each Value already includes information about every obstacle between that state and the goal, so we can safely go greedy on them. The Values make **present decisions optimal,** since the whole future from each state is encapsulated in its Value.

**Søren Kierkegaard** wrote that life can only be understood backwards, but it must be lived forwards. Dynamic programming has exactly this structure. The Values are understood backwards, calculated starting from the goal and moving toward the start. The decisions are lived forwards, made one at a time starting from A and moving toward J.

sections.title: Recursive breakdown and reconstruction

teaching.text: Dynamic programming starts by posing a problem, then its subproblems, then its sub- subproblems, and so on. The big problem is solved by solving the subproblems, and the subproblems are solved by solving the sub-subproblems.
In our network, the big problem is finding VAJ. Its subproblems are finding VBJ and VCJ. Their subproblems are finding VDJ ,VEJ, and VFJ. Their subproblems are finding VGJ, VHJ, and VIJ.

The breakdown continues until we reach a point where the problems are **trivial,** meaning they can be answered with no calculation at all. For G, H, and I, the answer is simply the cost of the one arrow to J.
Once the trivial problems are solved, we go back and solve the bigger problems, one level at a time, until we arrive at the original problem.

sections.title: The rule for propagating a value

teaching.text: The bigger problems are solved by **propagating Values** from each stage to the earlier stage using Bellman's idea. To propagate means to pass information along, and here the information moves from later stages to earlier ones.

**Bellman's rule** states that the Value at one state is the minimum of a set of numbers. Each number in the set is the sum of the cost to one of the next states and the Value at that next state. Every equation from VAJ down to VDJ ,VEJ, and VFJ follows this same pattern.
The rule is applied the same way at every stage.
children: The rule starts with the stage just before the goal, where the Values are known directly.
For each state in the stage before that, we list every arrow leaving it, add each arrow's cost to the Value of the state where that arrow ends, and keep the smallest sum as that state's Value.
Once a whole stage has Values, the same step is repeated for the stage before it.
The process stops when the starting state has its Value.

teaching.text: Each state needs only a handful of additions and one comparison, and each Value is calculated once and reused by every earlier state that connects to it. For example, V DJ = 13 is calculated once and then used in both the B equation and the C equation. This reuse is what keeps dynamic programming efficient when there are many stages and states.

sections.title: Least distance and least time can diverge

teaching.text: Dynamic programming tells us to **go through the bad 12 earlier** to get onto a route that does not get stuck later at the 9. Paying 12 to reach B instead of 7 to reach C looks like a mistake at the first step, but it puts us on the route with the lowest total. It may seem that making such a choice requires a big brain, since the decision-maker has to weigh the whole future against the present.
The same trade-off appears in the problem of a lifeguard reaching a person.
children: When the lifeguard and the person are both on sand, the lifeguard runs at a **constant speed** the entire way. The fastest route is then the **shortest path,** a straight line from the lifeguard to the person. This holds whether the person is directly across the sand or off at an angle along the beach.

When the person is in the water, the speeds are **different.** The lifeguard runs fast on sand but swims slowly in water. The **path of least time** is no longer a straight line. The lifeguard runs a longer distance along the sand, reaching the water at a point closer to the swimmer, and then swims a short distance. The route bends at the water's edge.

teaching.text: The lifeguard's best route accepts a longer stretch of running, which looks worse by distance, to cut down the slow and costly swimming later. This is the same structure as paying 12 early to avoid the 9 at the end.

sections.title: Refraction shares the least-time principle

teaching.text: **Decision-making is like physics.** Light shows the same behavior as the lifeguard, in the case of **refraction,** which is the bending of light as it passes from one material into another.
children: Light travels **faster in air** and **slower in water.**
When light passes between air and water, its path bends at the surface, just as the lifeguard's route bends at the water's edge.

This bending is why a pencil standing in a glass of water appears broken or bent at the water line. The light coming from the underwater part of the pencil changes direction at the surface before reaching the eye.

teaching.text: Light takes a path shaped the way the lifeguard's best route is shaped, with a bend at the boundary between a fast region and a slow region. Light has no brain at all, so choosing a route that accepts an early cost to avoid a larger later one does not require a big brain. Physical systems arrive at these optimal paths on their own, and dynamic programming describes the same kind of optimal route through a series of stages.

sections.title: Reading the completed state values

teaching.text: The complete solution can be written directly on the network by labeling each state with two things: its **Value** and the **best next state** to move to.
children: A is labeled 30 and B. The best cost from A is 30, and the best move is to B.
B is labeled 18 and D. C is labeled 24 and E.
D is labeled 13 and G. E is labeled 14 and G. F is labeled 15 and G.
G, H, and I are labeled 5 and J, 9 and J, and 8 and J.

teaching.text: With these labels, the best route can be read off by starting at A and following each state's best next state: A to B, B to D, D to G, and G to J, for a total of 30.

The labels also give the best route from **any** state, not just from A. If we somehow ended up at C, the labels tell us to go to E, then G, then J, and that the cost from C will be 24. A single backward calculation solves the problem for every possible starting point at once.

sections.title: Pop quiz heading
Learning and coffee share approach to equilibrium

teaching.text: A learning process can be tracked by plotting a quantity x against **epochs,** where an epoch is one round of learning in which the value of x gets updated. The **learning rate** controls how large each update is, and here it is set to 10%.
Three runs of the process start from different **initial conditions,** abbreviated **IC,** which are the starting values of x.
children: The run with IC = 130 starts high and drops quickly toward about 80.
The run with IC = 10 starts low and rises quickly toward about 80.
The run with IC = 80 starts at about 80 and stays there.
Within roughly the first 25 to 50 epochs, all three runs meet, and from then until epoch 300 they fluctuate together in a narrow band around 80.

teaching.text: The final value does not depend on where the process starts. The initial condition only changes the early part of the curve, while the long-run behavior is the same for all three runs. The changes are fastest at the beginning, when x is farthest from 80, and they slow down as x gets closer.
Coffee changing temperature in a room follows the same pattern, tracked as temperature in °C against time in minutes over 8 minutes, with **room temperature at 18°C.**
children: Three cups of **hot coffee** start at 100°C, 80°C, and 60°C. All three cool toward room temperature, and by 8 minutes they are at roughly 29°C, 26°C, and 23°C.
Three cups of **iced coffee** start at 10°C, 5°C, and 0°C. All three warm toward room temperature, and by 8 minutes they are all close to it, at roughly 16°C to 17°C.

The hot coffee starting at 100°C drops much faster at first than the one starting at 60°C. The larger the gap between the coffee and the room, the faster the temperature changes, and the change slows down as the gap shrinks.

teaching.text: In both systems, many different starting values move toward the same final value: about 80 for the learning process and 18°C for the coffee. The speed of change depends on how far the current value is from that final value.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 3
Homework reminder
Position and velocity change each other

teaching.text: A **harmonic oscillator** is built from only two quantities, x and v. We can think of x as how far something is displaced from its resting point, and v as its **velocity,** which is how fast and in which direction x is moving. Neither variable is interesting alone. The whole system is about **how x and v change over time as a result of their relation to each other.**

To talk about change over time, we put a dot over a variable. ẋ means the change in x as time increases, and v̇ means the change in v as time increases. This way of writing rates of change is **Isaac Newton's notation.**
children: The sign of the dotted quantity tells us the direction of change. When ẋ is positive, x is rising, and when ẋ is negative, x is falling.
The same rule holds for v. A positive v̇ means v is rising, and a negative v̇ means v is falling.
The size of the dotted quantity tells us how quickly the change happens. A large positive ẋ means x is climbing quickly, and a small positive ẋ means it is climbing slowly.

teaching.text: The defining feature of the harmonic oscillator is that x **and v change each other.** The rate at which x changes is set by v, and the rate at which v changes is set by x. Neither variable can change on its own terms, and this two-way dependence is what produces repeating back-and-forth motion.
The first equation says that the rate of change of x equals the current value of v: ẋ = v
The second equation says that the rate of change of v equals the negative of x: v̇ = −x

sections.title: Read the sign of the change

teaching.text: When v is positive, ẋ is positive, so x rises.
When v is negative, ẋ is negative, so x falls.
In other words, v directly steers x. Whatever sign v has at a given moment is the direction x moves at that moment.
When x is positive, v̇ is negative, so v falls. As v keeps falling, it eventually becomes negative, and through the first equation that negative v makes x fall back down.
When x is negative, v̇ is positive, so v rises. Once v becomes positive, the first equation makes x rise back up.
Suppose that at some moment v equals −5. Substituting into the first equation gives: ẋ = v = −5
The rate of change of x is negative, so x **will go down.**
The value of x itself does not matter for this conclusion. Only the sign of v decides whether x is rising or falling.
Now suppose that at some moment x equals −5. Substituting into the second equation gives: v̇ = −x = −(−5) = 5
The two minus signs cancel, so the rate of change of v is positive, and v **will go** UP.
This is the restoring behavior in action. When x is below zero, v is pushed upward, and an upward v will then lift x back toward zero through the first equation.
The example shows why x and v must be read together. Knowing v tells us what x is about to do, and knowing x tells us what v is about to do.

sections.title: Two different sign relationships

teaching.text: The **minus sign** is the heart of the system. It means v is always pushed in the direction opposite to wherever x currently is.

Putting the two equations together, whenever x moves away from zero in either direction, the second equation turns v around, and the first equation then carries x back toward zero. This **restoring relationship** is what keeps the system from drifting off and instead makes it swing back and forth.

sections.title: Follow the position–velocity cycle

teaching.text: We can follow the system moment by moment, starting with x at its highest positive value and v equal to zero.
children: At the start, x is positive, so v̇ is negative and v begins to drop below zero. As soon as v is negative, ẋ is negative, so x starts to decrease. At first x decreases slowly, since v is only slightly negative.
While x is still positive, v keeps getting more negative. A more negative v makes x fall faster, so x drops more and more steeply.
When x reaches zero, v̇ equals zero, so v stops decreasing. At this instant v is at its most negative value, which means x is crossing zero at its fastest speed.
Once x is below zero, v̇ becomes positive, so v starts rising back toward zero. x is still falling, but more and more slowly.
When v returns to zero, x has reached its lowest, most negative value. At that point x stops moving down and turns around.

With x negative, v keeps rising and becomes positive, so x climbs. v reaches its largest positive value just as x crosses zero on the way up, and then x returns to its maximum as v comes back to zero. The system is now back where it started, and the whole cycle repeats.

teaching.text: Computing the system at a series of separate moments in time gives a sequence of points, where each new value of x and v is worked out from the values just before it. Connecting these points produces two smooth waves.
children: The x wave starts at the top, dips below zero to a lowest point, and climbs back up past zero to the top again.
The v wave starts at zero, dips below zero to its lowest point, returns to zero, and then rises above zero.
The two waves have the same shape but are shifted in time by a quarter of a cycle. v is at its extreme values exactly when x crosses zero, and v is zero exactly when x is at its extreme values.

sections.title: A closed feedback loop

teaching.text: The relationship can be drawn as a **loop of influence** with x and v each in a circle. One arrow runs from v to x, standing for ẋ = v, since v determines how x changes. A second arrow runs from x back to v, standing for v̇ = −x, since x determines how v changes.
The loop is closed, so a change in v changes x, and that change in x goes on to change v again.

A **dynamical system** is a set of variables together with rules for how those variables change over time. The x -v system is a specific kind called an **oscillation** or **vibration dynamical system.** Oscillation and vibration mean the same thing here: a quantity repeatedly swinging back and forth around a middle value.

The loop between x and v is enough, by itself, to generate this repeated swinging. x drives changes in v, and v drives changes in x, so once the system is set in motion it keeps cycling without anything outside it having to push it again.

Plotted against time t ,x traces a wave that starts at its peak, falls below zero, rises back to the same peak, and repeats. Each cycle reaches the same height and the same depth, and each cycle takes the same amount of time. v follows the same kind of repeating wave on its own axis over the same stretch of time.

sections.title: Homework reminder
Harmonic oscillators across systems

teaching.text: The same two-variable structure of ẋ = v and v̇ = −x shows up in a huge range of systems, including the air in the vocal tract, the vocal folds, economies, music, and matter itself.

Calling a system a harmonic oscillator means identifying something in it that plays the role of x, a displacement away from a resting state, and something that plays the role of v, the rate at which that displacement changes. It also means accepting a simplification, since real systems are usually messier than two perfectly linked variables. The harmonic oscillator is still useful as a model, since it captures the basic back-and-forth pattern that all of these systems share.

sections.title: Compression and rarefaction of air

teaching.text: The **vocal tract** is the air-filled passage from the vocal folds in the throat up through the mouth to the lips. We can picture a thin slice of air inside it, containing a large number of air particles.
**Pressure** in this slice depends on how close together the particles are.
children: **High pressure** means the air particles are very close together.
**Low pressure** means the air particles are very far apart.
The particles themselves stay the same. There are the same number of them, and each one is the same size. The only thing that changes is the distance between them.

teaching.text: **Compression** is the state in which particles are squeezed closer together than their normal spacing. **Rarefaction** is the state in which particles are spread farther apart than their normal spacing. The normal spacing, where the air is neither squeezed nor stretched, is the **equilibrium spacing.**
children: If we track one pair of neighboring particles, at equilibrium they sit at 100% of their equilibrium distance.
At the strongest compression, that pair is squeezed to about 56% of its equilibrium distance, so the particles are a little more than half as far apart as usual.
At the strongest rarefaction, the same pair is stretched to about 141% of its equilibrium distance.

The slice cycles continuously between these states. It compresses, passes back through equilibrium, rarefies, and passes back through equilibrium again. In real speech the motion is much smaller than these exaggerated values, and the slice is an idealized piece of the air.

teaching.text: The slice of air behaves like a harmonic oscillator. The spacing of the particles, measured relative to equilibrium, plays the role of x. Air that is squeezed together tends to push itself apart, and air that is spread out tends to be pulled back together, so any departure from equilibrium spacing is pushed back toward equilibrium. This is the same restoring relationship expressed by v̇ = −x, and it is why the slice keeps swinging between compression and rarefaction.

sections.title: Connect air motion to a cosine

teaching.text: The back-and-forth motion of the air slice follows a **cosine** function: x = cos(phase)
Here x measures the **normalized expansion** of the slice. Normalized means the values are scaled so that the largest stretch equals +1 and the largest squeeze equals −1.
children: x = +1 means the particles are **farthest apart,** which is maximum rarefaction.
x = 0 means the particles are at **equilibrium** spacing.
x = −1 means the particles are **closest together,** which is maximum compression.
Any positive value of x means the slice is rarefied to some degree, and any negative value means it is compressed to some degree.

teaching.text: The **phase** is the position within a cycle. One complete cycle corresponds to the phase increasing by 2π. Running the phase from 0 to 6π therefore covers exactly three full cycles, with the first cycle ending at 2π, the second at 4π, and the third at 6π.
Following one cycle in order:
children: At phase 0, the cosine equals +1, so the slice is at maximum rarefaction.
As the phase increases, x decreases. A value such as x = +0.74 means the particles are still farther apart than equilibrium, but less so than at the start.
At phase π/2, the cosine equals 0, so the slice passes through equilibrium.
A value such as x = −0.54 means the slice is now compressed, with particles closer together than equilibrium.
At phase π, the cosine equals −1, so the slice reaches maximum compression.
At phase 3π/2 ,x returns to 0, and at phase 2π ,x is back at +1, completing the pattern of maximum rarefaction, then compression, then rarefaction again.
Over the next two cycles, x passes through values such as +0.31 ,−0.05, −0.21, and +0.45, and each value's sign tells us whether the slice is rarefied or compressed at that moment.

teaching.text: The cosine is the same wave that the x -v system produces when x starts at its maximum and v starts at zero. In both cases the curve begins at the top and swings downward. So the vibrating air in the vocal tract is following the harmonic oscillator relationship, and its expansion over time traces a cosine.

sections.title: Vowels depend on tongue position

teaching.text: Vowels differ from one another in where the **tongue** sits inside the vocal tract. These positions can be imaged with magnetic resonance imaging, which produces a picture of the head cut down the middle from front to back, showing the lips, tongue, roof of the mouth, and throat. In these images the speaker faces left, the tongue is the large bright mass in the mouth, and the dark regions are air.

Vowels are organized along two dimensions. **Height** describes whether the tongue body is raised toward the roof of the mouth **(high)** or lowered **(low). Frontness** describes whether the tongue body is pushed forward toward the teeth **(front),** pulled back toward the throat **(back),** or held in between **(central).**
children: In **"dean,"** the vowel is **high and front.** The tongue body is raised and pushed forward, close to the hard roof of the mouth, which leaves a large open air space in the throat behind the tongue.
In **"dune,"** the vowel is **high and back.** The tongue is still raised, but its highest point is pulled back toward the soft rear part of the roof of the mouth.
In **"Dan,"** the vowel is **low and front.** The tongue is lowered and the mouth is more open, with the tongue body still positioned toward the front.
In **"Don,"** the vowel is **low and back.** The tongue is lowered and pulled back into the throat, which narrows the air space behind it.
In **"done,"** the vowel is **central.** The tongue rests in the middle of the mouth, neither strongly raised nor lowered and neither pushed forward nor pulled back.

teaching.text: Each tongue position gives the air in the vocal tract a different shape. A differently shaped column of air vibrates in a different way, and that difference in vibration is what makes one vowel sound different from another.

sections.title: Vowels combine more than one vibration

teaching.text: A single cosine describes air vibrating at one frequency. A vowel is more complex than that. The air in the vocal tract vibrates at **several frequencies at the same time,** and the vowel is the **sum** of those vibrations. Since each individual vibration is a cosine, and each cosine is the behavior of a harmonic oscillator, a vowel can be modeled as **harmonic oscillators added together.**

**Frequency** is the number of complete cycles a vibration makes per second, measured in **hertz (Hz).** A vibration at f hertz can be written as cos(2πft), where t is time in seconds. Multiplying by 2π converts the number of cycles into phase, since one full cycle equals a phase of 2π.
The vowel **/i/,** the vowel in "dean," is modeled as a combination of a 1 Hz vibration and a 4 Hz vibration: x(t) = cos(2πt) + cos(8πt)
The first term is the 1 Hz vibration, since 2π × 1 = 2π. The second term is the 4 Hz vibration, since 2π × 4 = 8π.
The result is a slow wave with fast ripples riding on top of it. Over 3 seconds, the slow component completes 3 cycles while the fast component completes 12 cycles.
The vowel **/a/,** the vowel in "Don," is modeled as a combination of a 2 Hz vibration and a 3 Hz vibration: x(t) = cos(4πt) + cos(6πt)
The first term is the 2 Hz vibration, since 2π × 2 = 4π. The second term is the 3 Hz vibration, since 2π × 3 = 6π.

Over 3 seconds, the 2 Hz component completes 6 cycles and the 3 Hz component completes 9 cycles. The two frequencies are close together, so the sum produces a different repeating pattern of tall and short swings than /i/ does.

These frequencies are **illustrative.** They are chosen low enough that the motion can be watched, and the two components in each vowel are given **equal amplitudes,** meaning each cosine swings between +1 and −1.
children: Since each component reaches at most +1 and at least −1, their sum ranges between +2 and −2.

The sum reaches +2 only when both cosines peak at the same moment. For both vowels this happens at t = 0, 1, 2, and 3 seconds, since every component frequency completes a whole number of cycles in each second.

At other moments the components partly cancel or partly reinforce each other. For example, /i/ can take a value like −1.21 at one moment while /a/ takes a value like +0.58, and at another moment /i/ can be at +0.62 while /a/ is at −1.62.

teaching.text: The same sign rule from the single cosine still applies. **Positive x means rarefaction,** with particles farther apart than equilibrium, and **negative x means compression,** with particles closer together. For /i/ and /a/, the slice of air in the vocal tract is squeezed and stretched in two different time patterns, and those two patterns are what distinguish the two vowels. Watching these patterns at one-quarter speed makes the different rhythms of squeezing and stretching visible.

sections.title: Praat demonstration

teaching.text: **Praat** is a free computer program used in phonetics to record and analyze speech. It displays the **waveform** of a recorded sound, which is the air pressure changing over time, and it can also break that sound into the frequencies it contains.

Recording vowels such as those in "dean" and "Don" in Praat shows the combined vibrations directly. Each vowel produces its own repeating waveform, and each waveform is made of several frequencies added together, which is the same idea as the two- frequency models of /i/ and /a/.

sections.title: Two vibrating parts of speech

teaching.text: During speech, **two things vibrate.** The first is the air in the vocal tract, which is the vibration modeled by the cosines and sums of cosines above. The second is the **vocal folds.**

The vocal folds are two folds of tissue in the **larynx,** the voice box in the throat. When air from the lungs pushes up against the closed folds, pressure builds until the folds are forced apart. Once they open and air rushes through, the pressure between them drops and the folds come back together. The cycle then repeats many times per second.
children: This repeated opening and closing is itself an oscillation, with the folds swinging away from their closed position and being pulled back again.
Each opening lets a puff of air through, so the vocal folds chop the steady airflow from the lungs into a rapid series of puffs.
Those puffs set the air in the vocal tract vibrating, and the shape of the vocal tract, set by the tongue position, determines which combination of frequencies that air vibrates at.

teaching.text: Speech sounds such as vowels therefore come from one oscillator driving another. The vocal folds vibrate, and the air in the vocal tract vibrates in response.

sections.title: Economic cycles around a growth trend

teaching.text: The harmonic oscillator pattern also appears in the **business cycle,** the repeated rise and fall of economic activity over time. The business cycle is plotted with **time** on the horizontal axis and the **level of real output** on the vertical axis. **Real output** is the total amount of goods and services an economy produces, adjusted so that price changes do not distort the comparison across years.
The business cycle moves through a repeating sequence of phases.
children: At a **peak,** output is at a high point.
During a **recession,** output falls.
At a **trough,** output reaches a low point.
During a **recovery,** output rises again until it reaches the next peak.
The sequence then repeats, moving from peak to recession to trough to recovery and back to peak.

teaching.text: The swings happen around a rising straight line labeled **trend** or **growth.** Over the long run, output tends to increase, so each later peak can be higher than the earlier one. The oscillation is the part of output that swings above and below this trend line.

To treat the business cycle as a harmonic oscillator, the distance of output above or below the trend plays the role of x. Output above the trend is followed by a fall back toward and below it, and output below the trend is followed by a rise back toward and above it, which is the same back-and-forth pattern produced by ẋ = v and v̇ = −x.

sections.title: Meadows reading reminder
Music and vibration

teaching.text: **Music is built from harmonic oscillators.** Every musical note is a vibration at a particular frequency. A plucked string, the column of air inside a wind instrument, and a vibrating reed each swing back and forth around a resting state, just as x does in the x -v system.
The **pitch** of a note corresponds to its frequency. A higher-pitched note vibrates more times per second, and a lower-pitched note vibrates fewer times per second.
Sheet music is a written record of which vibrations to produce and when. When several notes sound together, their vibrations add, the same way the 1 Hz and 4 Hz cosines add to form the model of /i/.

sections.title: Atoms, shell pictures and wave modes

teaching.text: The harmonic oscillator appears in physics at the scale of atoms as the **quantum harmonic oscillator.** In quantum physics, a vibrating system cannot vibrate with just any amount of energy. It can only take certain specific energy levels, which is what **quantized** means.

**Matter is made up of atoms with different numbers of electrons, some vibrating at a low frequency and some at a high frequency.** In the quantum description, electrons in an atom are not tiny balls on tracks but **wave modes,** which are specific allowed patterns of vibration.

**Magnesium** (Mg) shows two ways of picturing an atom. A neutral magnesium atom has 12 **electrons,** and its nucleus contains 12 **protons.** Its **ground-state configuration,** the arrangement of electrons at lowest energy, is written 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² .
children: In the older **"solar system" picture,** also called the **Bohr-style shell** picture, electrons are drawn as particles moving on circular paths around the nucleus. Magnesium's electrons are arranged in shells of 2, 8, **and 2: 2** electrons in shell 1, 8 electrons in shell 2, and 2 electrons in shell 3. This is a historical model of how the shells are arranged.

In the **quantum orbital picture,** each occupied wave mode, called an **orbital,** contributes a cloud of **electron density** around the nucleus. Darker shading indicates greater density, meaning a region where an electron is more likely to be found.

The **total electron density** of magnesium is built by adding together the densities of all its occupied orbitals: 1s², 2s², 2p⁶, and 3s² . The superscript counts the electrons in each orbital group, and 2p⁶ includes all three filled p orbitals. The sum is a sum of **probability densities,** and the sizes and shading contrasts of the orbitals are drawn schematically rather than to exact scale.
The innermost 1s electrons form the densest cloud close to the nucleus, the 2s and 2p electrons form a middle layer, and the 3s electrons form the faint outermost layer.

teaching.text: Atomic orbitals are **quantized wave modes,** which connects them to the idea of vibration, but **magnesium is not a harmonic-oscillator atom.** The quantum harmonic oscillator is a specific model, and real atoms like magnesium follow related but different rules. The electron configuration comes from NIST atomic data for magnesium, and the quantum model follows OpenStax University Physics Volume 3, sections 7.5 and 8.1.

sections.title: Python position–velocity demonstration

teaching.text: The x -v system can be computed step by step in Python, producing the same sequence of points traced through time in Section 4. The system starts with x at its maximum and v at zero, and time is divided into many small steps of size dt .
children: At each step, ẋ is set equal to the current v, following the first equation.
At the same step, v̇ is set equal to the negative of the current x, following the second equation.
The new x is the old x plus ẋ multiplied by the step size, and the new v is the old v plus v̇ multiplied by the step size.
Repeating this many times builds up the full x wave and v wave one small step at a time. Smaller steps make the computed points follow the true smooth waves more closely.

teaching.text: python
children: import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
dt = 0.01 # size of each time step
steps = 1000 # number of steps to compute
x = np.zeros(steps)
v = np.zeros(steps)
x[0] = 1.0 # x starts at its maximum
v[0] = 0.0 # v starts at zero
for n in range(steps - 1):
x_dot = v[n] # x-dot = v
v_dot = -x[n] # v-dot = -x
x[n + 1] = x[n] + x_dot * dt
v[n + 1] = v[n] + v_dot * dt
t = np.arange(steps) * dt
plt.plot(t, x, label="x")
plt.plot(t, v, label="v")
plt.xlabel("t")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

teaching.text: The plotted output reproduces the behavior of the harmonic oscillator. x starts at the top and traces a cosine wave, and v starts at zero, drops negative first, and traces the same wave shape shifted by a quarter of a cycle. v reaches its extremes whenever x crosses zero, and v passes through zero whenever x reaches its extremes.

sections.title: Dynamical Systems 5
Two quantities in an oscillator

teaching.text: A **harmonic oscillator** is a dynamical system with two variables that feed into each other: **position,** written x, and **velocity,** written v. Position tells us where something is, and velocity tells us how fast and in which direction it is moving. The system is fully described by two rules of change, one for each variable, and each rule depends on the other variable.
children: The dot above a letter is the notation for change over time. ẋ means the **increase or decrease in x with time,** so it is the rate at which position is changing at a given moment.
In the same way, v̇ means the **increase or decrease in v with time,** so it is the rate at which velocity is changing.

teaching.text: The first rule says that the rate of change of position is equal to the velocity: ẋ = v
This rule says that velocity drives position. When v is positive, x grows, and when v is negative, x shrinks. When v is exactly zero, x holds still for that instant.
In the loop diagram, this is the red arrow running from v to x, which marks v as the cause and x as the thing being changed.
The second rule says that the rate of change of velocity is equal to the negative of the position: v̇ = −x
This rule says that position drives velocity, but with a minus sign. When x is positive, velocity is pushed downward, and when x is negative, velocity is pushed upward.
This is the blue arrow running from x to v. Together, the red and blue arrows form a **closed loop of mutual influence: v** changes x, and x changes v, over and over.
We can work out what this loop does by stepping through it by hand, starting from x = 1 and v = 0. At the very start, position is at its highest value and nothing is moving yet.
children: Since x = 1, the second rule gives v̇ = −1, so velocity starts decreasing and becomes negative.

Once v is negative, the first rule says ẋ is negative, so position begins to fall. It falls slowly at first, since v has only just started to become negative, and then falls faster and faster as v grows more negative.

Position keeps falling until it crosses zero. At the moment x = 0, the second rule gives v̇ = 0, so velocity stops changing. This is the moment when velocity is at its most negative, which means position is falling at its fastest right as it passes through zero.
After the crossing, x is negative, so v̇ = −x is now positive. Velocity starts climbing back toward zero, which means position is still falling but falling more slowly.

When velocity reaches zero, position stops falling. This is the lowest point of x, at −1. From there, velocity turns positive, position starts to rise, and the whole sequence runs in reverse until x is back at +1 with v = 0.

teaching.text: Plotting both variables against time point by point gives two waves. Position starts at its peak of +1, drops through zero, bottoms out at −1, and comes back up to its peak.
Velocity starts at zero, dips negative, returns to zero, rises positive, and comes back to zero.
children: The two waves are offset from each other by a quarter of a cycle. **Velocity is zero whenever position is at a peak or a trough,** and **velocity is at its largest size whenever position is crossing zero.**
This offset is a direct consequence of the two rules. Position turns around only when velocity reaches zero, and velocity turns around only when position reaches zero.

sections.title: Repeated change in a loop

teaching.text: An **oscillation,** also called a **vibration,** is a repeating back-and-forth motion around a central point. The two-variable loop between x and v is the basic dynamical system that produces it. Each variable pushes on the other, and the result is that neither one ever settles down.
children: When the loop is drawn with one arrow from x to v and another from v back to x, it shows that the influence is **circular.** There is no single cause at the start and no single effect at the end.

Graphed smoothly over time, x traces a wave that starts high, swings down below zero, swings back up, and continues this pattern through repeated cycles. v traces a wave of the same shape that starts at zero and heads negative first, staying a quarter cycle out of step with x.

teaching.text: The key property of this system is that **it never comes to rest on its own.** In the systems from earlier dynamical-systems material, variables moved toward a resting value and stopped there. Here, every time one variable reaches its target, the other variable is at its largest value and pushes it past the target again.
children: This is why the motion keeps repeating. Position overshoots zero because velocity is at its maximum at the moment position reaches zero.
Velocity overshoots zero because position is at its maximum at the moment velocity reaches zero.

sections.title: Why a spring and a mass make vibration

teaching.text: Physically, vibration requires **two effects working together.** Neither one alone can produce a back-and-forth motion.

The first effect is a **spring,** more precisely a **viscous spring.** A spring is the springiness found in many objects around us, meaning their tendency to return to a natural shape or position after being pushed or pulled. The word "viscous" refers to a frictional, slowing quality, and it will be set aside here so that we can focus on the springiness itself.
children: A spring has a property called **stiffness.** Stiffness measures how strongly the spring pulls back toward its natural position when it has been moved away from it.
A very stiff spring pulls back hard, and a loose spring pulls back gently.

teaching.text: The second effect is **mass.** Mass is the amount of matter in an object, and it determines how the object carries motion once it is moving.
Vibration matters because it shows up across many different systems, both physical and abstract.
children: **The jolt we feel when a car hits a bump** is a vibration. The car's suspension springs and the car's mass together produce a bouncing motion.
**Music** is vibration. Strings, air columns, and drum skins all vibrate to produce sound.
**Boom and bust in economics** is a vibration. An economy swings above and below a steady level in repeating cycles.

**Oscillation in** SGD is a vibration. SGD stands for **stochastic gradient descent,** a method used to train machine-learning models by repeatedly nudging a value toward a target. Under some settings, that value swings back and forth around the target rather than settling onto it.
**The motion of the air in the vocal tract and the motion of the vocal folds during speech** are vibrations. Every sound we produce when we talk is built from these vibrations.

sections.title: Air particles move closer and farther apart

teaching.text: The air inside the vocal tract can be treated as a small slice of material made of many particles. During speech, the particles in the slice stay the same, and each particle stays the same size. **What changes is the distance between the particles.**
children: At **equilibrium spacing,** the particles sit at their natural, resting distance from one another. A chosen pair of neighboring particles is at 100% **of its equilibrium distance** at this point.
The equilibrium size of the slice serves as the reference that all other states are compared to.

teaching.text: **Compression** is the state in which the particles are pushed closer together than their resting distance. In a compressed slice, the chosen pair of particles sits at only 56% **of its equilibrium distance,** and the whole slice shrinks.
children: **High pressure means air that is packed very close together.** Compression is therefore a high-pressure state.

teaching.text: **Rarefaction** is the state in which the particles are spread farther apart than their resting distance. In a rarefied slice, the chosen pair sits at 144% **of its equilibrium distance,** and the whole slice expands.
children: **Low pressure means air that is spread very far apart.** Rarefaction is therefore a low-pressure state.

teaching.text: During speech, a slice of air in the vocal tract alternates between compression and rarefaction, shrinking and expanding around its equilibrium size again and again. This alternation is a vibration of the air.
children: The sizes used in this model are idealized and exaggerated so that the change in spacing is visible. Real air in the vocal tract changes its spacing by much smaller amounts.

sections.title: Balancing feedback reduces displacement

teaching.text: The spring effect on its own can be written as a single rule of change: ẋ = − 1/3 x

Here x is the distance of the spring from its natural position, and ẋ is how fast that distance is changing. The rule says the rate of change is always **one third of the current distance, with the opposite sign.**
The sign of x decides which way the spring moves.
children: **If x is positive, ẋ is negative, so x falls.** A spring stretched in the positive direction moves back toward zero.
**If x is negative, ẋ is positive, so x rises.** A spring compressed in the negative direction also moves back toward zero, just from the other side.

teaching.text: We can follow the rule step by step starting from an **initial condition** of x = 1. The initial condition is the value the system starts from before any change has happened.
children: With x = 1, the rule says x will fall, and it will **fall by one third of its current size.** One third of 1 is 1/3 , so x drops to: 1 − 1/3 = 2/3

teaching.text: The same rule then applies again to the new value. One third of 2/3 is 2/9 , so x drops to: 2/3 − 2/9 = 4/9
Applying the rule once more, one third of 4/9 is 4/27 , so x drops to: 4/9 − 4/27 = 8/27
The process repeats **again and again,** and each drop is smaller than the one before it. The first drop was 1/3 , the second was 2/9 , and the third was 4/27 .
**When x is smaller, ẋ, its speed of falling, is smaller too.** The spring moves quickly when it is far from its natural position and slows down as it gets closer.
children: When graphed against time, x starts at 1 and curves downward toward zero. The slope of the curve is steeply negative at the start and becomes **smaller and smaller negative** as time goes on.
The curve gets closer and closer to zero but **never crosses it.** There is nothing in this rule that could carry x past zero, since the speed shrinks to nothing as the distance shrinks to nothing.

teaching.text: If the initial condition is negative, the same logic runs in the opposite direction. Starting below zero, x rises toward zero, quickly at first and then more and more slowly, with a slope that is **smaller and smaller positive.** It approaches zero from below and again never crosses it.

This kind of system has a **natural resting condition,** which here is x = 0. When the system's position is at a **discrepancy** with its natural position, meaning it has been moved away from where it rests, it **feeds back on itself** through the rule ẋ = − 1/3 x to cancel that discrepancy. This is the idea of **negative feedback,** also called **balancing feedback,** from Meadows' work on systems.
children: The feedback is called negative because the change always opposes the discrepancy. A positive discrepancy produces a negative change, and a negative discrepancy produces a positive change.
It is called balancing because its effect is to bring the system back into balance at its resting point.

teaching.text: **These are systems that are in motion only in order to achieve their equilibrium.** An **equilibrium** is a state where the system has no reason to change any further. A spring moves only because it is away from its natural position, and once it arrives there, all motion stops.
The number − 1/3 in the rule is what we call **stiffness.** Its size controls how quickly the spring returns to equilibrium.
children: A **higher stiffness,** such as a larger fraction than one third, means the spring closes a bigger share of the remaining distance at every step, so it returns to zero faster.
A **lower stiffness,** such as a smaller fraction than one third, means the spring closes a smaller share of the remaining distance at every step, so it returns to zero more slowly.

sections.title: Mass carries motion onward

teaching.text: Mass behaves very differently from a spring. **If a mass is moving, it just keeps on moving.** A mass does not need a discrepancy or a target to keep going, and it has no natural resting position that it is trying to reach.

This principle was worked out by **Galileo, Descartes, and Newton: a mass in motion stays in motion.** Without an outside force acting on it, a moving object continues at the same speed in the same direction.
children: Motion of this kind is called **constant velocity.** An object with constant velocity covers **the same distance in every equal interval of time.**
A car rolling along a straight street past buildings and trees at constant velocity moves past the same amount of scenery in every moment. It does not speed up, slow down, or stop on its own.

teaching.text: This property is exactly what the spring lacks. A spring slows down as it nears its resting point and stops there, while a mass carries its motion forward regardless of where it is.

sections.title: Returning to a place versus passing through it

teaching.text: The difference between the two effects can be stated in one line: **a spring stops at a place, while a mass stops after a process.** The spring's stopping point is a location, its natural position. A mass does not stop at a location at all, and it keeps moving until something removes its motion over time.

Consider a spring attached to a wall on one end, lying on a table, with no mass on its free end. Its displacement x is **measured from the spring's natural position,** which is set as x = 0, and the scale runs from −1 to +1.
children: When the free end is pulled out to +1 and released, the spring **returns and stops at x = 0.** The end approaches zero **without crossing it.**
Graphed over time, this return from +1 is a curve that starts at +1 and bends down toward zero, flattening out as it gets close. It has the same shape as the curve produced by ẋ = − 1/3 x.
When the free end is instead pushed to −1 and released, **x rises toward zero without crossing it.** The curve starts at −1 and bends up toward zero, again flattening as it arrives.
Pulling the spring out again gives the exact same return each time. A spring alone always settles at its natural position and never overshoots.

teaching.text: When a **mass** is attached to the free end of the same spring and the system is released from +1, the result is completely different. The spring still pulls the mass back toward zero, but when the mass reaches zero it is moving at its fastest, and **the mass carries that motion through the crossing.**
children: The mass continues past zero into negative displacement. Now the spring is stretched the other way, so it pulls back toward zero from the negative side. The mass slows down, stops near −1, and is pulled back through zero toward the positive side again.
This repeats through **every crossing.** The mass keeps going back and forth past the natural position rather than stopping at it.

teaching.text: Graphed over time, the spring-plus-mass system produces a **lightly damped oscillation.** The curve swings from +1 down below zero, back up above zero, and continues swinging through repeated cycles.
children: **Damping** is the gradual loss of motion over time, which comes from the viscous, frictional part of the spring. In a lightly damped system, the damping is small, so each swing is only a little smaller than the one before it and the oscillation continues for many cycles.
Eventually, the damping would bring the mass to rest at zero, which is what it means for a mass to stop after a process. The stopping happens only at the end of a long sequence of swings.

teaching.text: Putting the two effects together recovers the harmonic oscillator. The spring supplies the pull back toward the natural position, which is the rule v̇ = −x: the farther the mass is from zero, the harder its velocity is pushed back toward zero. The mass supplies persistent motion, which is the rule ẋ = v: position keeps changing as long as there is velocity, including at the moment the mass passes through zero.
children: A spring alone gives balancing feedback that ends at equilibrium.
A mass alone gives motion that never turns around.
**A spring and a mass together give vibration,** since the spring keeps turning the motion around and the mass keeps carrying it past the resting point.

sections.title: Air expansion follows a cosine

teaching.text: The vibration of a slice of air in the vocal tract can be described with a single mathematical function, the **cosine.** The value x here measures the **normalized expansion** of the slice, meaning how far the particles are spread relative to their equilibrium spacing, scaled so that the extremes are +1 and −1. x = cos(phase)
x = +1 means the particles are **farthest apart,** which is **maximum rarefaction.**
x = 0 means the particles are at their **equilibrium** spacing.
x = −1 means the particles are **closest together,** which is **maximum compression.**

The **phase** is the input to the cosine, and it tracks where the slice is within its cycle of motion. One full cycle of the cosine takes a phase of 2π, so a phase running from 0 to 6π covers exactly **three cycles.**
children: At a phase of 0, the cosine equals +1, so the slice starts at maximum rarefaction.
At a phase of π, the cosine equals −1, so the slice has reached maximum compression halfway through the first cycle.
At a phase of 2π, the cosine is back at +1, so the slice has returned to maximum rarefaction and completed Cycle 1. The same pattern repeats for Cycle 2, ending at 4π, and Cycle 3, ending at 6π.

teaching.text: The slice therefore moves from **maximum rarefaction to compression and back to rarefaction** in every cycle, following the cosine curve exactly.
children: Partway through a swing, the slice is in an in-between state. At x = +0.84, the particles are still rarefied, farther apart than at equilibrium but not at their maximum spread. At x = −0.84, the particles are compressed, closer together than at equilibrium but not at their tightest.

teaching.text: This cosine is the same wave that position traced in the harmonic oscillator, starting at its peak and swinging down through zero to its lowest point and back. The air in the vocal tract behaves as a harmonic oscillator, with the springiness of the air pushing it back toward equilibrium spacing and the mass of the air carrying it past equilibrium each time.
children: The sizes of the slice in this model are exaggerated and its motion is slowed, so that each stage of the cycle is visible. The dashed boundary marks the slice's equilibrium size.

sections.title: Compare tongue configurations for vowels

teaching.text: Different vowels are made by placing the tongue in different positions inside the vocal tract. Side-view MRI images of the head during five words show how the tongue body moves to create each vowel. The vowels are organized along two dimensions: **height,** which is how high or low the tongue body sits in the mouth, and **front/back,** which is how far forward or backward the tongue body sits.
**High vowels** are made with the tongue body raised close to the roof of the mouth.
children: In **"dean,"** the vowel is **high and front.** The tongue body is pushed up and forward toward the hard palate, which leaves a wide open space in the throat behind the tongue.
In **"dune,"** the vowel is **high and back.** The tongue body is raised but bunched toward the back of the mouth, closer to the soft palate.

teaching.text: **Low vowels** are made with the tongue body lowered away from the roof of the mouth.
children: In **"Dan,"** the vowel is **low and front.** The tongue sits lower in the mouth while staying toward the front, leaving a large open space above it.
In **"Don,"** the vowel is **low and back.** The tongue is lowered and pulled back toward the throat, which narrows the space behind the tongue.

teaching.text: In **"done,"** the vowel is **central.** The tongue body sits in a middle position, neither pushed far forward nor pulled far back.

Each tongue position gives the air inside the vocal tract a different shape. A different shape changes how the air vibrates, and those differences in vibration are what make one vowel sound different from another.

sections.title: Frequency counts cycles in a fixed interval

teaching.text: The **frequency** of a vibration is how many complete cycles it goes through in a given amount of time. Three vibrations can be compared over the same 12-second interval, with each one covering the same range of particle spacing and each one starting at **maximum rarefaction,** where x = +1.
children: x = +1 is maximum rarefaction, x = 0 is equilibrium, and x = −1 is maximum compression, just as in the single cosine.

teaching.text: The **low-frequency** vibration completes 3 **cycles in 12 seconds.** Each cycle takes 4 seconds, so its peaks at +1 fall at 0, 4, 8, and 12 seconds. Measured in cycles per second, its frequency is: 3 cycles/ 12 s = 0.25 cycles per second

The **mid-frequency** vibration completes 6 **cycles in 12 seconds.** Each cycle takes 2 seconds, so the slice swings between rarefaction and compression twice as often as the low-frequency one. Its frequency is: 6 cycles/ 12 s = 0.5 cycles per second

The **high-frequency** vibration completes 9 **cycles in 12 seconds.** Each cycle takes 12/9 , or about 1.33 seconds, so this slice swings the most rapidly of the three. Its frequency is: 9 cycles/ 12 s = 0.75 cycles per second

All three vibrations reach the same extremes of rarefaction and compression. **The only thing that differs among them is how quickly the cycle repeats.** Frequency is therefore a separate property from how far the particles spread or squeeze, and a vibration can be made faster or slower without changing its range.
children: One cycle per second is called **one hertz,** written **Hz.** This unit is used for the frequencies in the vowel models.

sections.title: Different combinations give different vowel patterns

teaching.text: A vowel is not a single cosine. A vowel can be modeled as **a sum of vibrations at different frequencies happening at the same time** in the same slice of air. The simplest model uses two frequencies of equal size added together, and the two frequencies chosen give each vowel its own pattern of motion.
children: The frequencies in these models are small illustrative values, chosen so the combined wave is easy to follow. They are not the actual frequencies found in speech.

teaching.text: A cosine at a frequency of f Hz can be written as cos(2πft), where t is time in seconds. Since one cycle takes a phase of 2π, multiplying 2π by f gives f full cycles for every second that passes.
children: A 1 Hz vibration is cos(2πt), which reaches a phase of 2π, or one full cycle, at t = 1 second.
A 4 Hz vibration is cos(8πt), which reaches a phase of 8π, or four full cycles, at t = 1 second.

teaching.text: The vowel **/i/,** the vowel in "dean," is modeled as a 1 **Hz vibration plus a 4 Hz vibration:** x(t) = cos(2πt) + cos(8πt)
At t = 0, both cosines equal +1, so the sum is: x(0) = 1 + 1 = 2
This means the combined wave starts at +2, which is **maximum rarefaction** for the combined motion. The range of x is now from +2 to −2, since two waves of size 1 are stacked together.
At t = 0.5 seconds, the 1 Hz wave is halfway through its cycle and the 4 Hz wave has completed exactly two cycles, so the sum is: x(0.5) = cos(π) + cos(4π) = −1 + 1 = 0

Between its large peaks, the /i/ wave has a busy pattern: it rises to smaller peaks near +1, dips down to troughs near −1.7, and touches zero at the halfway point. The fast 4 Hz wave rides on top of the slow 1 Hz wave, putting several smaller wiggles inside each slow cycle.
The whole pattern repeats **once every second,** returning to +2 at 1, 2, and 3 seconds.
The vowel **/a/,** close to the vowel in "Don," is modeled as a 2 **Hz vibration plus a 3 Hz vibration:** x(t) = cos(4πt) + cos(6πt)
At t = 0, both cosines equal +1, so /a/ also starts at x = +2, which is maximum rarefaction.
