children: **Time runs along the horizontal axis**, and **frequency runs up the vertical axis**.
**Amplitude is shown as darkness**, so high amplitude is **black**, medium amplitude is **gray**, and low amplitude is **white**.
So a formant appears as a **dark band** at its frequency.

teaching.text: In a spectrogram of **/ia/**, the dark bands follow the formants over time.
children: During **/i/**, **F1 is very low and F2 is very high**, so there is a dark band low down, a gap, and another dark band high up, with the two formants **far apart**.
Moving into **/a/**, the formants **come close together**, as the low band rises and the high band falls.

sections.title: Reflection prompt
Wide harmonic spacing makes formants harder to identify

teaching.text: **Formants can only be seen through the harmonics they shape**, so the spacing of the harmonics matters a great deal.
children: When the harmonics are closely spaced, each formant has **lots of harmonics to shape**, so each formant band is easy to see.
When the harmonics are widely spaced, far fewer of them fall near each formant, and **it becomes very hard to tell harmonics from formants.**

teaching.text: Holding the vocal tract filter fixed and changing only **F0**, the base frequency of the vocal folds, makes this clear.
children: A **low F0** gives **dense** harmonics that trace each formant band well.
A **higher F0** gives **sparser** harmonics, so a formant can fall **between** them.
A **very high F0** gives so few harmonics that the formants may look like **isolated harmonics** instead of bands.

So **the formants are a smooth envelope and the harmonics are samples of it, and a higher F0 gives fewer samples.** Raising F0 does not move the formants, but it leaves fewer harmonics to reveal them.

teaching.text: High voices make this a real problem for listeners too.
children: **A toddler's harmonics are widely spaced**, so it is hard to tell where their formants are unless the listener is used to how that toddler speaks.
**A soprano's first harmonic is very high**, and with so few harmonics near the formants, most people cannot follow the words at an opera, even while watching the singer's lips.

sections.title: Homework 4 lab reminder
Speech → Neural Networks
Five membrane modes combine into one motion

teaching.text: Speech has **two major vibrating systems**, and the first is the **vocal folds**. They are a **membrane fixed on all sides**, made of a whole bunch of masses and springs, and they vibrate in many modes.
children: In **Mode 1**, all the masses go up and down together.
In **Mode 2**, half of them go up while the other half go down.
Higher modes split the membrane into more and more parts going against each other.
This is literally what happens in the throat during speech, and measuring the spectrum of real voices confirms it.

teaching.text: Because the vocal folds are **fixed on all sides**, their frequencies are **harmonics**, which are **whole-number multiples** of the lowest one. **The lowest harmonic is called F0.** Each person has a different F0, but every voice has its harmonics stacked at multiples of its own F0.

A membrane is easy to break down into modes, and its modes are named by **how many moving regions it has in each direction**, such as **(1, 1)** for one region and **(2, 2)** for four regions. The frequencies given to its modes in the picture are assigned for teaching rather than worked out for the membrane. Added together, the separate motions make one complicated surface, and its spectrum at a pickup point has **equal spikes**, one for each mode.

sections.title: A fixed end and a free end select odd harmonics

teaching.text: The second major vibrating system is fixed differently, so it follows a different rule, and a **string fixed at the bottom and free at the top** is the simplest version of it.
children: At the **fixed bottom**, the string cannot move, so that point is a **node**.
At the **free top**, the string moves the most, so that point is an **antinode**.
So every mode must have a node at the bottom and an antinode at the top.

teaching.text: Because of those ends, **only the odd harmonics occur**, at one, three, five and seven times the lowest frequency. With equal excitation of each mode, the spectrum at the free end has **equal spikes** at those odd multiples.
For a string of the **same length and wave speed**, switching from **fixed at both ends** to **fixed at only one end** **halves the lowest frequency**.

sections.title: Quarter-wavelength packets explain the allowed modes

teaching.text: A **quarter-wave packet** is the piece of a wave that runs from a **node to an antinode**. That piece is exactly what joins the fixed bottom to the free top, so each mode is built out of these packets.
children: **Mode 1** holds just **one packet**, so it vibrates at the lowest frequency.
**Mode 2** holds **three packets**, so it vibrates three times as fast as Mode 1.
**Mode 3** holds **five packets**, and **Mode 4** holds **seven packets**, so they vibrate five and seven times as fast.

teaching.text: The counts are always **odd**, because the string must still end with an antinode at the top. Adding one packet would leave a node there, so packets get added **two at a time**, and **more packets in the same length means shorter waves and faster vibration.**

sections.title: Air moves longitudinally in vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: The second vibrating system is the **air in the vocal tract**. Picture the space inside the mouth and throat straightened out into a tube, with the flesh of the tongue, the palate and the throat forming its walls.
children: The air is **fixed at the glottis**, the space between the vocal folds, because the folds are closed and the air cannot move back and forth there.
The air is **free at the lips**, where it can go **in and out** over and over.
So the air in the vocal tract is fixed at one end and free at the other, and its frequencies are **formants** that fall at **odd multiples**.

teaching.text: The air can be modeled as a **mass-spring chain that is fixed at one end and free at the other**, with **identical masses** in a **uniform tube**.
children: **Mode 1 corresponds to F1**, the **lowest air mode** of the tube.
**Mode 2 corresponds to F2**, the **next air mode**, and it vibrates **three times faster** than Mode 1.

Three spots are marked along the tube, measured from the glottis. The spot **one third of the way** up is labeled **/a/**, the spot **two thirds of the way** up is labeled **/i/**, and the **lip end** is labeled **/u/**.

sections.title: Track air motion separately from compression

teaching.text: The air does **two different things** at different places, and both can be seen directly.
children: Where the slivers of air **come very close together and then move far apart**, the air is **compressing and expanding**, so it is acting as a **spring**. That happens at the **closed end**, because air can be squeezed against something closed.
Where the slivers stay **equally spaced** and just **move back and forth**, the air is acting as a **mass**. That happens at the **open end**, because there is nothing there to squeeze against.

teaching.text: **In every mode, the air at the open end acts like a mass**, going back and forth with hardly any expansion, and **the air near the closed end always acts like a spring.**

sections.title: Compare positions within an air mode

teaching.text: **Constricting the tract at a springy spot raises the formant of that mode.** Take a spot in the **third mode** where the air is bunched up and expanding, so it is very springy, and reason through what a constriction does there.
children: **A constriction always increases both mass and stiffness**, because squeezing air makes it stiffer, the way squeezing a tire does, and bunching it up makes it effectively heavier.
At this spot the air is **acting like a pure spring**, with no back-and-forth movement and only compression and expansion.
So the **mass does not matter** there, and only the **added stiffness** counts, and since added stiffness raises frequency, **F3 goes up**.

This chain of reasoning has to be built fresh at each spot, because the situation is slightly different everywhere, so following the logic step by step matters more than memorizing the answer for one spot.

sections.title: Vowel positions change where the tract is narrowed

teaching.text: Real images of speaking come from an **MRI** that films the vocal tract during speech, and the images reveal **where each vowel squeezes the air**.
children: **High** and **low** describe how high the tongue is, while **front**, **central** and **back** describe how far forward it is.
In **Dean**, the tongue is **high and front**, which makes a constriction **two thirds of the way from the glottis**.
In **Dune**, the tongue is **high and back**, and the vowel has a constriction **at the lips**.
In **Done**, the tongue is **central**, and the tract has **no constriction** at all.
In **Don**, the tongue is **low and back**, which squeezes the air **far back in the throat, one third of the way from the glottis**.
In **Dan**, the tongue is **low and front**.

teaching.text: **Combining these images with the model** is where theory meets reality. The model treats the air as masses and springs that are fixed on one side and free to move on the other, and a constriction is drawn as **stiffer springs and heavier masses** at that spot. Where each vowel puts its constriction decides which formants go up and which go down.

sections.title: A constriction changes inertia and restoring stiffness

teaching.text: **Compressing air raises its stiffness**, so **constricting at a place with lots of compression raises the frequency**.
**Bunching up air raises its mass, or density**, so **constricting where the air moves a lot adds mass**, and that **lowers the frequency**.

sections.title: Use both modes to interpret the same tract location

teaching.text: **So making a constriction increases both mass and stiffness**, but that does **not** mean the effects cancel and constrictions leave frequency unchanged. **The parts of a vibrating medium that move the most alternate with the parts that compress and uncompress the most**, so at any given spot in a mode, one effect wins.
children: If the air there is mostly **moving**, the added **mass** wins and the formant **goes down**.
If the air there is mostly **compressing**, the added **stiffness** wins and the formant **goes up**.
The same constriction can do opposite things to different formants, because each mode has its own pattern of motion and compression.

sections.title: Lip loading lowers both F1 and F2 in the /u/ model

teaching.text: For **/u/**, the **lips squeeze the air** at the free end, which is called **loading the free end**, and that raises both the mass and the stiffness of the air at the lips.
**The air at the open end acts like a mass in every mode.** It goes back and forth with hardly any squeezing, because there is nothing there to squeeze against.
children: So the added **stiffness does not matter**, because there is no compression or expansion there.
The added **mass does matter**, because the air there is moving a lot.
**Increasing mass where the air moves lowers the frequency**, so **both F1 and F2 go down**.

teaching.text: This is what happens in the mouth for vowels like the ones in **dune, moon and through**, and measurements match it. Starting from schwa, a student's **/u/** had an **F1 far below the F1 of schwa**.

sections.title: A front constriction separates the effects on F1 and F2

teaching.text: For **/i/**, the air is squeezed **two thirds of the way from the closed end**, and the two modes are doing different things at that spot.
children: In **Mode 1**, the air there is **mostly moving back and forth**, so it acts like a **mass**.
In **Mode 2**, the air there is **mostly compressing**, so it acts like a **spring**.

teaching.text: **A constriction always raises both mass and stiffness**, so the outcome depends on which one matters in each mode.
children: **F1 goes down**, because the air is moving and the added mass wins.
**F2 goes up**, because the air is compressing and the added stiffness wins.
So **wherever stiffness is what matters, the frequency goes up, and wherever mass is what matters, the frequency goes down.**

teaching.text: Moving from schwa into /i/ in a recording, **F1 drops and F2 rises**, exactly as predicted. If this were not real, no one could tell what anyone else was saying.

sections.title: A back constriction reverses the F1 and F2 pattern

teaching.text: For **/a/**, the air is squeezed **far back, about one third of the way from the closed end**.
children: In **Mode 1**, that spot is **close to the closed end**, and **near the closed end there is always springiness**, so the added stiffness wins and **F1 goes up**.

In **Mode 2**, everything alternates, with compression near the closed end, compression further up, and **the motion of the mass in between**, right where /a/ squeezes, so the added mass wins and **F2 goes down**.

teaching.text: **The vowel /a/ is the opposite of /i/**, with **F1 up and F2 down**. Students who measured their own /a/ found a high F1 and an F2 not far above it, which fits the prediction.

sections.title: Air motion and compression in the vocal-tract modes

teaching.text: In **Mode 1**, the air is **very springy at the closed end**, then less and less springy and **more and more like a mass** toward the open end. In **higher modes**, springiness and mass **alternate** along the tube, and they repeat more times the higher the mode is.

sections.title: The vocal-fold source sets harmonic spacing

teaching.text: The **vocal folds** differ from person to person, and the **rules for mass and stiffness** predict their F0.
children: **Big, loose, heavy vocal folds** have **high mass and low stiffness**, so their **F0 is low** and their harmonics are packed closely together.
**Tighter, lighter vocal folds** give a **higher F0**, with the harmonics spaced farther apart.
**Very tight, light vocal folds** give an even **higher F0**, with the harmonics spaced farther apart still.
So a lower F0 packs **more harmonics** into the same range of frequencies, and a higher F0 spaces them **farther apart**.

teaching.text: **F0 is not fixed during speech**, because only a robot keeps F0 constant, and real speech **changes F0 all the time**, in every vowel.
children: "The dog slept here" and "The dog slept here?" differ mainly in **F0**, which **goes down** at the end of the statement and **goes up** at the end of the question.
Speakers change F0 by **changing the stiffness of the vocal folds** with the muscles in the larynx.
Listeners use those changes in F0 to understand meaning, and even to tell when someone is **sarcastic** or **pretending**.

sections.title: The vocal-tract filter favors nearby harmonics

teaching.text: The **air in the vocal tract** has its own formants. For **schwa**, the tube has no constriction, so its formants sit at the evenly spaced odd multiples that a uniform tube predicts.
children: The exact values vary with **how long the vocal tract is** and **how heavy and stiff the air is**, which depends on many factors, such as how wet the vocal tract is.
Compared with schwa, **/u/** moves F1 and F2 **both down**, **/i/** moves **F1 down and F2 up**, and **/a/** moves **F1 up and F2 down**.

teaching.text: **Formants are all about where the constriction is in the vocal tract**, and they interact with the harmonics by one core rule. **A formant encourages the closest harmonics to be audible, and harmonics far from that formant are muted.**
children: Harmonics that sit near a formant get **amplified**.
Harmonics further from the formant get weaker, and those far away **will not be audible** to a listener.

teaching.text: **The shape of the vowel is the filter, because the voiced source supplies the harmonics and the filter chooses which harmonics survive.** Formants do not make new frequencies, but instead decide which of the source's harmonics come through strongly, and each vowel's formant targets match its constriction.
children: **Schwa** has its formants evenly spread up the spectrum.
**The vowel /u/** has a low F1 and a low F2.
**The vowel /i/** has a very low F1 and a very high F2, so its first two formants are far apart.
**The vowel /a/** has a high F1 and a fairly low F2, so its first two formants sit close together.

sections.title: One filter can look different at different pitches

teaching.text: **This interaction between source and filter is really important.** Picture a person with **heavy, loose vocal folds**, whose harmonics are closely spaced, saying **schwa**.
children: There are **lots of harmonics near the first formant**, so the ones closest to it are **amplified**, while those farther away get weaker.
Between the two formants, the harmonics get **weaker**.
Near the second formant, the harmonics get **amplified** again.
So **the lower F0 is, the more harmonics the formants have to shape.**

teaching.text: Now picture **very light, very stiff vocal folds**, whose harmonics are widely spaced. The first formant may have **no harmonic close by to amplify**, and **sparse harmonics can miss a formant or make it look ambiguous**, which is why some students had a hard time finding their formants in lab.
Two everyday cases come from this mismatch.
children: **Opera singers** have such a high F0 that their **formants barely line up with any harmonics**, so listeners can hardly hear which vowels they are making, and opera is hard to understand. Singers are taught to shape their mouths so that their harmonics line up with their formants, often by opening the mouth wide like a smile.
**Very small children** have a very high F0, and their formants and harmonics line up so poorly that only their caretakers, who are used to their speech, can easily follow them.

teaching.text: **F0 can be measured in Praat** by taking a spectral slice of a vowel and selecting the lowest harmonic. For a measured male voice, the next harmonic came out at about **double** the first, so the theory holds.

sections.title: Map spectra into a spectrogram

teaching.text: **A spectrum captures one instant, and a spectrogram stacks many spectra over time.** Two things change in the spectrogram.
children: **Time runs along the horizontal axis, and frequency runs up the vertical axis.**
**How dark a spot is tells how much energy, or amplitude, there is**, so high amplitude is **black**, medium amplitude is **gray**, and low amplitude is **white**.
So a formant appears as a **dark band** at its frequency, and its rise and fall over time can be followed.

teaching.text: Speech is **not one steady vowel**, because speakers are constantly changing sounds, so **the formants are constantly changing**. In the spectrogram of **/ia/**, the lowest band **rises** from /i/ to /a/, so F1 goes up, and the next band **falls**, so F2 goes down.

sections.title: Reflection prompt

teaching.text: A recording of **"Where were you a year ago?"** follows the same rules.
children: Where **F2 rises high**, the speaker is making a sound like **/i/**. The squeeze of air near two thirds raises F2 and lowers F1, so **/i/ is the classic vowel with a low F1 and a high F2**.
In **"you,"** **all the formants go down**, just as /u/ predicts.
Across the whole phrase, the formants keep going up and down as each sound is made, so everything in the theory appears in real speech.

sections.title: Speech-complexity experiment prompt

teaching.text: **One experiment reveals how complex listening to speech really is.** A speaker recorded the syllables **"ma"** and **"na,"** the **m** sound was **cut out of "ma,"** the **a** vowel was **cut out of "na,"** and the two pieces were **pasted together**, so an m from "ma" was followed by an a from "na."
children: Since the consonant came from "ma," the result should sound like **"ma."** Instead, **it sounds like "na."**

teaching.text: **Listeners decide which consonant they heard mostly from the vowel that follows it**, because the formants of the vowel differ depending on the consonant before it.
children: In the **a that follows m**, the formants stay **fairly stationary**.
In the **a that follows n**, one formant **drops sharply**.
That drop in a formant inside the vowel is what tells the listener "n," so it **overrides** the m that was pasted in front.

teaching.text: **Speech perception does not decide sound by sound, slice by slice.** Listeners take in **a whole stretch of speech** and then decide what they heard, often deciding about a consonant **later in time**, during the vowel.
children: For decades, speech recognition machines failed because they were built to recognize each little piece separately, the way people think they listen.
**An AI that understands speech has to be complex enough to use later information to decide about earlier sounds**, and this is why large language models were needed for speech recognition.

sections.title: Use formants as input to vowel recognition

teaching.text: A **neural network** can be **trained on formants** to **decide which vowel is being spoken**. The **W's**, which are the weights, contain the **knowledge** in a neural network, and training adjusts them until the network makes good decisions.

sections.title: A fully connected linear vowel network

teaching.text: This network only multiplies and adds, with **no activation functions**. It takes **two inputs**, passes them through **three hidden layers**, and ends in **five outputs**.
children: The **two inputs** are **F1 and F2**, the frequencies of the first two modes of the air's vibration, measured from spectrograms.
Each hidden layer **does inner products**, multiplying the incoming numbers by the W's and adding them up, and so makes a new **representation** of the input.
This is like information arriving at the ear and then being processed by one part of the brain after another before the brain decides what it heard.
The **five outputs** are **/done/, /dune/, /dean/, /Don/ and /Dan/**, with one neuron for each vowel.

sections.title: Random weights assign signed contributions to connections

teaching.text: The example input has **a very low F1 and a very high F2**, and **a very low F1 with a very high F2 is the pattern for /i/**, so a smart network should decide **dean**.
**Before training, every weight is a random number between negative one and one.** A positive weight pushes the next neuron up, and a negative weight pushes it down.

**Training is what fixes the bad W's.** The network is told the right answer as a distribution with all of its probability on dean and none on any other word, and **stochastic gradient descent** then changes each weight. The next time the same formants come in, the inner products should make the value for **dean** higher than all the others.

sections.title: Forward flow and an illustrative output distribution

teaching.text: In **forward flow**, the input flows forward through the network one layer at a time.
children: Each neuron in the first layer multiplies F1 and F2 by its own weights and adds the products, and **none of these calculations have to be done by hand.**
That gives three numbers, which pass through the next weights to give two numbers, and those pass through more weights to give four numbers.
Those four numbers pass through the last weights to give the **output, which is a probability distribution over the five words**.

teaching.text: The output puts the **most probability on done** and spreads the rest over the other four words.
children: The values **add up to one**, so it is a **good probability distribution**.
But it says **"done,"** while the vowel was **/i/**. **The W's are bad**, so the network is "stupid" before training, and the result is met with an angry face.

sections.title: Declare the layer sequence in PyTorch

teaching.text: The same network can be written in **Python** using **PyTorch**. The code imports **torch** and **torch.nn as nn**, and it builds the network inside **nn.Sequential**, which means **a sequence of layers** that the numbers pass through in order.
Each layer is an **nn.Linear**, which says how many numbers the layer takes in and how many it gives out.
children: The first layer, **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, says that it is a layer that takes **two inputs** and makes **three outputs**.
The next layer, **nn.Linear(3, 2)**, takes those **three** numbers and makes **two**.
The layer after that, **nn.Linear(2, 4)**, takes **two** numbers and makes **four**.
The last layer, **nn.Linear(4, 5)**, takes **four** numbers and makes **five**, one for each vowel.
Each layer's output size has to match the next layer's input size, so that the numbers can flow all the way through.

teaching.text: Each **nn.Linear** holds a weight matrix with **one row for each receiving neuron** and **one column for each incoming value**. Setting **bias=False** removes the bias, an extra constant added to a neuron's sum, so each layer only multiplies and adds, just as in the diagram.
This code is **only a declaration, with no training**, because it describes the network the way the machine sees it. It does not yet feed in any formants or change any weights.

lecture15.title: Neural Networks · Forward propagation, learning, and sigmoid

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: **A neural network is a numerical processing machine**, which means it takes in numbers, processes them, and **makes a decision**. This one is a very rudimentary **speech recognizer**, because it takes the **formants** measured from vowels in lab and decides **which vowel was spoken**.
children: The two **input neurons** just take information from the environment, with one taking **F1** and the other taking **F2** for one person's vowel.
The five **output neurons** stand for the words **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
Between them are **three hidden layers** of neurons, which are called **hidden** because they are neither the input nor the output.

teaching.text: **The weights are the network's knowledge.** Every connection between two neurons has a **weight**, a positive or negative number often written **W**, and everything the network "knows" about vowels is stored in these numbers.
children: The network is **fully connected**, so every neuron sends a connection to every neuron in the next layer.
The weights in the diagram are made up for teaching, and they **stay fixed** while the network works out its answer.
**A positive weight pushes the next neuron up, and a negative weight pushes it down**, and the **bigger** the weight, the stronger the push.

teaching.text: The weights leaving the formants are **tiny**, while the deeper weights are **much larger**. The formants are big numbers in the hundreds and thousands of hertz, so tiny weights are enough to turn them into modest values for the rest of the network.

**How many layers and neurons a network should have is not known in advance.** With **no hidden layers**, and the inputs wired straight to the outputs, the network would most likely keep making mistakes. **More numbers give the network more freedom**, so as those numbers improve, it can capture something as hard as recognizing a vowel from just two numbers, and in practice people try the simplest design first, see how it performs, and then add more.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** is how the network makes a decision, with the input traveling forward through the layers one layer at a time. The example input is a vowel with a **low F1 and a high F2**. There are **no biases**, meaning no extra constants added in, and the hidden neurons are **linear**, so each one passes its sum straight on.

**Each neuron computes an inner product.** It multiplies each incoming number by the weight on that connection and then **adds** the results, so for the top neuron of the first hidden layer, the inner product is w₁ F1 + w₂ F2
children: Here w1 is the weight on the connection from F1, which is small and positive, and w2 is the weight on the connection from F2, which is small and negative.

teaching.text: With the example formants, the F1 part adds a small amount and the F2 part takes away a bit more, so the result lands **just below zero**.
children: That number is the neuron's **activation**, and here it is called a **linear activation**, because nothing else is done to it.
**None of these calculations ever have to be done by hand**, because what matters is understanding what is happening.

teaching.text: **The same thing repeats at every layer.** The activations of one layer become the inputs to the next layer, which does more inner products with its own weights, and the network keeps going through all three hidden layers until it reaches the output. Each layer has to wait for the one before it, so **a change at the input ripples all the way through**.
**Knowledge has been reduced to positive and negative numbers, and making a decision uses nothing but multiplying and adding**, which is arithmetic from second grade.
children: The word **inference** means figuring out a decision, and almost all of its work is done by **simple numbers that hold the knowledge** together with **addition and multiplication that do the inferring**.

This is one of the most surprising facts about AI. Emulating human cognition might seem to need incredibly complex math, but the systems people talk to all the time use only these elementary operations.

teaching.text: **This idea did not come out of nowhere.** The brain is a **chemical and electrical machine**, and over the last century or so, scientists discovered that its chemistry performs operations like **addition and multiplication**, so the operations inside a neural network are close to what the brain actually does.

After the last layer, the final numbers have to be **turned into a probability distribution**. **A probability distribution is a set of numbers that add up to one**, and those numbers are **the network's decision**.
children: Each number is how sure the network is about one vowel, so a value of one tenth means a **ten percent chance** that the formants were for that vowel.
**Probabilities go from zero to one, and percentages go from zero to a hundred, but they are the same idea.**

teaching.text: The operation that turns the final numbers into probabilities is called **softmax**. pᵢ = exp(zᵢ) / (Σⱼ exp(zⱼ))
children: Here zi is one output's raw score, and pi is its probability.
**Softmax just converts numbers into probabilities.** It makes every score positive and divides each one by the shared total, so all five add up to one.
**A bigger score always ends up as a bigger probability**, and if one word's score goes up, the probabilities of the other words have to go down.
The details of the calculation do not need to be known, because what matters is that **the probabilities add up to one** and **what they mean as a decision**.

teaching.text: For the example vowel, the network gives **done a little over half of the probability**, which is **much higher than any other vowel**, so **the network decides it heard "done."** The highest probability is always the decision.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation

teaching.text: The network's decision can be reasoned about without calculating anything. Take the **top neuron of the last hidden layer**, whose activation is **positive**, and its connection to **done**, whose weight is also **positive**.
**If that activation goes up, the probability of done goes up.**
children: The activation enters done's inner product multiplied by that weight.
Both numbers are **positive**, so their product is positive.
A bigger activation makes that positive contribution **bigger**, which **raises** done's score and so raises its probability.

teaching.text: **If that weight goes up, the probability of done also goes up**, for the same reason. Everything in that product is positive, so making either number bigger makes the contribution bigger.

**Every question like this comes down to the inner product.** When two positive numbers are multiplied, the result is positive, and making either one bigger **increases** that neuron's contribution to the probability. The point is never to work out what one decimal times another comes to, but **always to see what actually happens to the decision.**

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **This network is "stupid,"** and in fact **all neural networks start out stupid**, because they start with **random weights**, which means they know nothing. This one decided "done," but the formants were actually for **/i/, as in dean**.
**A network becomes smarter only by being told the right answer**, and the right answer is given as a **desired output**.
children: The desired output for dean puts **no chance on done, dune, Don or Dan and all of the chance on dean**.
A target written with **zeros everywhere and a single one** is called a **one-hot encoding**.

In practice, nobody sits there saying "right" or "wrong." Instead the network gets a table of data, where each row says, for example, that when this person produced these two formants, the vowel was dean.

teaching.text: The output the network actually produced is called the **computed output**, and the gap between it and the desired output is the **error**. Here the network gave dean only a small chance when it should have given dean all of it, so the error is large.
**Backpropagation** is the algorithm that **changes all the weights** so that the network becomes a little smarter.
children: The goal is to **pump up the probability of the right answer** toward one and push the wrong ones down toward zero.
This can work because the decision is made entirely by inner products, so if the weights change, the products change, and so does the decision.

**Learning is gradual, just as in stochastic gradient descent.** The network does not learn the right answer all at once, but sees one example, changes its weights **a little**, sees another, changes them a little more, and so on.

teaching.text: The rule for updating a weight moves it a small step in the direction that lowers the error. W ← W - η (∂L / ∂W)
children: Here W is a weight and L is the error, also called the **loss**, and the fraction tells **whether nudging that weight up would raise or lower the error**.
The symbol η is the **learning rate**, which sets the size of each step.
**The minus sign moves each weight in whichever direction makes the error smaller.**

teaching.text: The new weights are worked out **from the output backward**, so the connections into the outputs change first, then the ones into the third hidden layer, then the second, and then the first. **Forward propagation** sends information forward through inner products, while **backpropagation** sends the corrections backward, and during the backward pass the forward activations stay as they were and are reused.
children: The weight from the positive neuron into **dean** gets **bigger**, which adds more to dean.
The weight from that same neuron into **done** gets **smaller**, which takes away from done.
The weights leaving the formants **barely change**, because they use a much smaller step size to match the large values in hertz.

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** is the algorithm that changes all the weights so the network makes better decisions, and it is made of two algorithms. **Stochastic gradient descent** improves each weight gradually, the same way SGD improved an estimate of an average, and it has the same learning rate. **Dynamic programming** decides the order, so the last weights get improved first and the earlier ones after.

Comparing two outputs gives the error. The **computed output** is what the network produced, putting most of the probability on done and only about 8 percent on dean. The **desired output** is the right answer, with a one for dean and zeros everywhere else.
The difference between them is the **error**, or **loss**, and more probability on dean means less error.
The error says exactly how each output should move, so done's probability should go down, dean's should go up, and the others should go down.

**The weights are changed from the end backward.** First come the connections into the outputs, then into the third hidden layer, then the second and then the first, while the activations from the forward pass stay fixed and are reused.
The weight from the positive neuron into dean gets bigger, the weights from the negative neurons into dean get smaller, and the weight from the positive neuron into done gets smaller.
The weights leaving the formants barely move, because they use a much smaller step to match the large hertz values.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: For any weight, the same thing always has to be asked. **If this weight goes up, will the error go up or down?** Comparing two marked weights makes the difference clear.
**The positive weight from the last hidden neuron to done is an easy problem.**
children: Done's probability comes from an inner product that includes that weight times the neuron's positive activation.
**If the weight goes up**, that contribution grows, done's probability goes **up**, and the network gets **more wrong**, since done should have no probability at all.
**So the weight should go down**, because a smaller weight shrinks that contribution and pulls done's probability **down** toward zero.
This is a crystal-clear decision, because there is only **one inner product** between that weight and the probability.

teaching.text: **The weight from F1 to the first hidden layer is a hard problem.**
children: Changing it changes the activation of its neuron in the first layer.
That changes the activations in the second layer, which change the third layer, which finally change the probabilities.
At every step, the change mixes with **many other weights and activations**, some pushing one way and some the other.

So **its effect on the decision is mediated by all of the calculations in between**, and it is very hard to tell just by looking whether it should go up or down, although backpropagation still works it out.

teaching.text: For any weight, the question is the same. **If this weight goes up, will the error go up or down?** Two marked weights make the comparison.

**The weight from the last hidden layer to done is an easy problem.** Done's large probability comes from an inner product that includes this weight times a positive activation of about 1.57. If the weight went up, that contribution would grow, done's probability would go up, and the network would get more wrong, since done should be zero.
So the weight should go down, because a smaller weight shrinks that contribution and pulls done's probability down.
There is only one inner product between this weight and the probability, so the decision is crystal clear.

**The weight from F1 to the first hidden layer is a hard problem.** Changing it changes the activation of its first-layer neuron, which changes the second layer, which changes the third layer, which finally changes the probabilities.
At every step, that change mixes with many other weights and activations, some pushing one way and some the other.
Its effect on the decision is mediated by all the intermediate calculations, so just looking at it, there is no way to tell whether it should go up or down. Backpropagation still works it out.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Why the weights are changed from the end backward is guaranteed to be on the exam.** The answer comes from comparing the **last weights**, labeled **W5**, with the **first weights**, labeled **W2**.
**Improving the last weights, W5, is easy.**
children: **The output probabilities are directly determined by the last weights**, and so **the error is very directly determined by the last weights** as well.
So the error between the computed and desired outputs can be used **directly** to decide how to change W5.

teaching.text: **Improving the first weights, W2, is hard.**
children: **W2 affects its own activations, which then affect another two layers of activations along with many other weights.**
So it is **really hard to figure out how much blame W2 deserves** for mistakes made all the way at the end.
Moreover, **the effect of W2 on the errors includes the effect of W5**, since W5 is downstream of W2, and any change in W2 has to pass through W5 to reach the output.

teaching.text: A strong exam answer explains that **changing an early weight's influence on the probabilities is a much more involved and mediated set of calculations, while changing a last weight changes the probabilities right away.** So the last weights pose a **simple, trivial problem**, while the early weights pose a **complex, big problem that already includes the effect of the later ones**.
**When a problem contains smaller and smaller problems inside it, the algorithm to use is dynamic programming.**
children: **Dynamic programming** solves the **easiest, most trivial problem first**, then uses its answer to solve the next bigger one, and so on up to the hardest.
It comes from **Bellman** and **Viterbi**, so **backpropagation is Bellman and Viterbi's dynamic programming** applied to neural networks.

So **backpropagation is SGD plus dynamic programming.** SGD changes each weight **gradually**, a little at a time, and dynamic programming gives backpropagation its **"back,"** since it improves the last weights first, then the next, then the next, all the way back to the first.

teaching.text: **For years people said brains could never do something as neat as a clean forward pass followed by a clean backward pass**, because brains are messy chemistry, but **that turned out to be wrong**. Research has since found that a **single brain neuron works much like a forward process followed by a backward one**, so choices that AI engineers made were already built into nervous systems long ago.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: To train the network, it has to be told **the desired output for every input**, and that information is given as **two matrices**. **A matrix is just a table of numbers**, and both tables come from the class's own lab data, with one row for each recording.
The **input matrix, Formant_Inputs**, has one row for each recording and two columns.
children: Each row holds **one recording's two formants**, F1 and F2.
It has **two columns because the network takes two numbers in**.

teaching.text: The **target matrix, TrueVowel_Outputs**, has one row for each recording and five columns.
children: Each row is a **one-hot answer**, with a one in the column of the true vowel and a zero everywhere else.
It has **five columns because the network decides among five vowels**, in the order done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.

teaching.text: **The rows of the two tables must line up**, because row by row they describe the same recording.
children: If the first row of formants comes from a recording of **done**, the first row of the target has to say done.
The tables effectively tell the network that if it gets one pair of formants it had better say one vowel, and if it gets another pair the answer is a different vowel, and that holds for every row.
If one table were reordered and not the other, the network would learn from wrong answers.

teaching.text: The rows on display are only a sample, not the full dataset. The network keeps its own **computed output**, but the **target never changes**, and training compares the two and changes only the **weights**.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: A short **Python program** trains this network. It looks mysterious at first, but each part has a plain meaning, and **the code never has to be written from scratch**, because what matters is what each line **does**, not its brackets and punctuation.
**The import lines bring in a library.**
children: The line **import torch** means **use the PyTorch library**, and **from torch import nn** brings in its neural network tools.

A **library** is code that someone else already wrote, so a programmer does not have to write every step. The library does all the background work, which means a network can be described in just a few lines.
So **these lines bring into Python everything needed for doing inner products and backpropagation**, which means anyone can build these networks without solving backpropagation themselves.

teaching.text: The command **torch.load** reads the two saved tables from files, the formants and the one-hot answers. **Load** means to bring information in, which is the same thing that happens when a file is double-clicked, and **.float()** turns the values into decimal numbers.
**The command nn.Sequential means that the network is a sequence of layers**, one layer after another. That is the most basic kind of neural network, and it describes every network built so far.
**The command nn.Linear means a layer that does inner products by multiplying and adding.**
children: The first layer, **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, takes **two inputs** and produces **three outputs**, so it is the first hidden layer.
The next layer, **nn.Linear(3, 2)**, takes **three** numbers and produces **two**.
The layer after that, **nn.Linear(2, 4)**, takes **two** numbers and produces **four**.
The last layer, **nn.Linear(4, 5)**, takes **four** numbers and produces **five**, one for each vowel.

teaching.text: **The network has five layers but only four Linear lines**, because the **input layer does no processing** and just receives numbers. Only layers that do inner products get a line, so the input layer appears only in the first line's statement that it takes two numbers.
The **last lines are the only lines PyTorch needs for learning**, and their words are recognizable.
children: The word **SGD** stands for **stochastic gradient descent**, and it is given a **learning rate**, which sets the size of each step.
The command **zero_grad()** clears out the old leftover corrections.
The **loss** is **the mistake**, the gap between the computed and desired outputs, and **CrossEntropyLoss** measures it while handling the probability part itself.
The command **backward()** is **backpropagation**, which works out how each weight affects the mistake.
The command **step()** actually **changes the weights**.
This program takes just **one step using all of the rows** together, so it is a **minimal example** rather than a full training run.

teaching.text: The program starts from **PyTorch's own default weights**, not the hand-picked ones in the diagram, so it has the same shape but different weights and would not reproduce the diagram's numbers.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **Neural networks did not come out of nowhere**, because their most basic features come from **discoveries about animal brains**.
children: Neuroscientists discovered that there are **neurons**, so artificial networks have neurons.
They discovered that **each neuron collects information from many other neurons**, and that is exactly what the **inner product** does.

teaching.text: **Adrian** discovered that **neurons are nearly digital**, which means that **they either fire or they do not fire.**
children: A real neuron's activation is not some in-between number, because it is basically **off or on**.
The neurons in the vowel network are not like that, since their activations can be any number at all, with no limit.

teaching.text: **The sigmoid** is an **activation function** that was added to neural networks to copy Adrian's discovery. A **linear** neuron just passes on its plain inner product, while the sigmoid takes that inner product and turns it into a number **between zero and one**. σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
children: Here z is the inner product, and σ(z) is the neuron's new activation.
**If the inner product is large and positive, the sigmoid is near one, and if it is large and negative, the sigmoid is basically zero.**
So a fairly negative inner product and a hugely negative one both come out almost at zero, and a fairly positive inner product and a hugely positive one both come out almost at one.
In this way **the sigmoid digitizes neural processing**, making artificial neurons work like real ones, close to off or close to on.

teaching.text: Without this kind of limit, real neurons would have no ceiling, but **the brain's chemistry keeps neurons either off or on**, and the sigmoid copies that.

**Animal perception reflects this S shape too.** **Some things that seem alike are perceived as different, and some things that are very different are perceived as the same**, and the S shape of the sigmoid produces both.
children: In the **steep middle**, two inputs that are close together come out **far apart**, so they are perceived as different.
Out on the **flat ends**, two inputs that are very different come out **nearly the same**, so they are perceived as the same.

teaching.text: **AI is duplicating the abilities of animals.** Engineers took each discovery about animal brains and built it in, then added their own ideas, such as other functions shaped somewhat like the sigmoid. **People often say that AI has nothing to do with human cognition, but that is false**, because a big reason it works is that it copies our own abilities, using math as simple as multiplying and adding.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: The sigmoid can be added to the vowel network **one hidden neuron at a time**, keeping **the same input and every weight the same**. Each hidden neuron switches from **linear** to **sigmoid** in layer order, and **the outputs still go through softmax**, so they stay probabilities that add up to one.
The first neuron to switch has an inner product **just below zero**, which sits on the steep middle of the curve.
children: So the sigmoid gives a value **just under one half**.
That means the neuron now sends a **positive** number where it used to send a **negative** one.

teaching.text: **After each switch, everything that comes after it is recalculated.** Later neurons get their inputs from earlier ones, so once an earlier activation changes, **every later inner product changes too**. That is why the old linear numbers cannot simply be run through the sigmoid one at a time, since each new value has to come from the updated layer before it.
As the neurons switch, **the network's answer moves.**
children: At first it decides **done**, with a clear majority.
As the first layer switches, done's lead shrinks until **done and Don are nearly tied**.
When the second layer switches, **Don** takes the lead, and then **Dan** does.
With **every hidden neuron on sigmoid**, every hidden activation is between zero and one, **Dan is on top**, **dean has risen to second place**, and **done has dropped well behind**.

teaching.text: **Only the activation rule changed and no weight moved, so this is not learning.** Even so, the decision changed completely, and because **dean still is not the top answer**, the sigmoid changes how the network behaves without making it correct.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The program becomes a sigmoid network by adding **nn.Sigmoid()** after each hidden layer. **The command nn.Sigmoid means apply the sigmoid, which means make the neuron digital**, and it goes after **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, **nn.Linear(3, 2)** and **nn.Linear(2, 4)**.

**The sigmoid changes the values but not how many there are.** A layer that produces three numbers still produces three after the sigmoid, so the next layer still fits and the network keeps exactly the same shape.
**The last layer, nn.Linear(4, 5), has no sigmoid**, because its five outputs go to the loss, which turns them into probabilities.
children: The **sigmoid** squeezes **each hidden neuron on its own** toward off or on.
The **softmax** turns **all five final scores together** into a decision that adds up to one.

teaching.text: The training lines stay the same as before. The program starts from PyTorch's own default weights, so it would not reproduce the diagram's exact numbers, and in lab the sigmoid can also be swapped for **other functions**, such as one called **ReLU**, to discover whether they make vowel recognition better or worse.

lecture16.title: Neural Networks · Vowel data, training runs, and initialization

sections.title: Neural Networks
Two formants feed a fully connected network

teaching.text: This **neural network** simulates a very simple piece of human perception. It takes the **two formants**, F1 and F2, of an isolated vowel and **decides which vowel it is**, and its five possible answers are **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
children: The **two input neurons** take F1 and F2 from the environment.
**Three hidden layers** of neurons process those two numbers.
The **five output neurons** give the decision, with one neuron for each vowel.
Every neuron connects to every neuron in the next layer, so the network is fully connected.

teaching.text: **The weights are the network's knowledge**, and each one is a positive or negative number. A **positive** weight pushes the next neuron up, a **negative** one pushes it down, and the **bigger** the weight, the stronger the push. The weights in the diagram are made up for teaching, and they stay fixed while the network makes a decision.
Learning works by telling the network the right answer.
children: At first **the weights are random**, so the network "doesn't know anything" and its decisions are stupid.
The right answer is given as a **probability distribution**, so for a recording of dean it puts all of the probability on dean, meaning the network should be **completely sure it was dean**.
That target is usually very different from the distribution the stupid network produces at first. The difference is a **mistake**, and the network learns by correcting its mistakes.

sections.title: Forward propagation combines weighted inputs

teaching.text: **Forward propagation** carries one input through the network to a decision. The example vowel has a **low F1 and a high F2**, and it is one person's /i/.

**Every step is an inner product**, which means multiplying each incoming number by its weight and adding the results, so for the top neuron of the first hidden layer, the inner product is w₁ F1 + w₂ F2
children: Here w1 is the weight from F1, which is small and positive, and w2 is the weight from F2, which is small and negative.
The F1 part adds a little and the F2 part takes away a little more, so this neuron's **activation** lands **just below zero**.
The other neurons do the same thing with their own weights, and layer by layer the activations become the inputs to the next inner products, until the network reaches a decision.
Since the two weights point in opposite directions, **a higher F1 pushes this neuron up and a higher F2 pushes it down**.

teaching.text: **The last numbers are turned into a probability distribution**, a set of numbers that **add up to one**, and the operation that does this is called **softmax**. pᵢ = exp(zᵢ) / (Σⱼ exp(zⱼ))
children: Here zi is one vowel's final score, and pi is its probability.
Softmax makes every score positive and divides each one by the total, so **a bigger score always gives a bigger probability** and all five add up to one.
Raising one vowel's score **lowers the probabilities of the others**, since they all share the same total.

teaching.text: With these weights, **done gets the highest probability, a little over half**, so **the network decides "done."** But the correct answer is **dean**, so the network's knowledge is wrong and it has to change its weights.

sections.title: Pop quiz · Forward propagation
Vowel formants overlap across five categories

teaching.text: The vowel data from the class's own lab is plotted with **F1 along one axis and F2 along the other**, with hundreds of recordings and the same number for each vowel. **Each vowel forms a cloud of points**, since the same vowel comes out a little differently every time.
**Some of the patterns are clear.**
children: **The vowel /i/, as in dean**, sits apart with a **high F2 and a low F1**, as the theory predicts.
**The vowel /ae/, as in Dan**, spreads toward **high values of F1**.
So /i/ is clearly different from /u/, the vowel of dune.

teaching.text: **But there is a lot of overlap.**
children: **The vowels of dune, Don and done crowd into the same region**, with a middle F1 and a fairly low F2.
So a new speaker whose formants land in that region could be saying any of the three.

Some points are probably **errors**, but real data always has errors, just as talking to an AI on a train has background noise and a photo in bright sun has glare. Those points stay in the data because **that is what real life is like**.

teaching.text: **This overlap is why AI is hard.** If every vowel sat in its own separate spot, recognizing vowels would be easy, but instead a network has to see the data **many times** to learn what really separates the vowels. **No setting of the weights can separate recordings that land on top of each other**, because two formants are all the network gets.
This overlap was discovered when **Peterson and Barney** measured the vowels of many speakers from spectrograms.
children: They found an **enormous overlap** between vowels and realized that speech recognition would be far harder than anyone expected.

For decades, people tried to write programs to solve it, including trying to **normalize** away the differences between speakers, but **none of it worked**, and what finally worked was **a neural network trained with backpropagation**.

teaching.text: **Static vowels turned out to be harder than moving speech.** For years, everyone predicted that a **static** problem like this one, with two formants from one moment, would be easy, and that **dynamic** speech, with formants always changing, would be very hard. **Everyone turned out to be wrong**, because large language models deal with very dynamic information and work much better, since they use information from before and after each moment.

sections.title: Info on Exam 2 and Exam 3
Backpropagation uses the difference between prediction and target

teaching.text: **Backpropagation** is the algorithm that **changes all the weights** so that the network makes better decisions, and it is made of **two algorithms** working together.
children: **Stochastic gradient descent (SGD)** improves each weight **gradually**, in the same way that SGD improved an estimate of an average from data, and it has the same issues, including a **learning rate**.
**Dynamic programming** decides the **order**, so the last weights get improved first, then the ones before them, and so on back to the start.

teaching.text: **Comparing two outputs gives the error.**
children: The **computed output** is what the network produced, which here puts most of the probability on done and only a small amount on dean.
The **desired output** is the right answer, with all of the probability on dean, and a target with a single one and zeros everywhere else is called a **one-hot target**.
The difference between them is the **error**, also called the **loss**. Here the loss depends on how much probability went to dean, so **more probability on dean means less error.**

teaching.text: The error says exactly how each output should move. **The probability of done should go down, the probability of dean should go up, and the probabilities of the other vowels should go down.**
Each weight is changed with the **update rule**. W ← W - η (∂L / ∂W)
children: Here W is a weight and L is the loss, and the fraction tells **whether raising that weight would raise or lower the error**.
The symbol η is the **learning rate**, which is the size of each step.
**The minus sign moves each weight in whichever direction lowers the error.**

teaching.text: **The weights are changed from the end backward**, starting with the connections into the outputs, then the connections into the third hidden layer, then the second, and then the first. The activations from the forward pass stay fixed and are reused.
children: The weight from a positive neuron into **dean gets bigger**, so it adds more to dean.
The weights from the negative neurons into dean **get smaller**, so they take less away from dean.
The weight from that same positive neuron into **done gets smaller**, which lowers the wrong answer.
The weights leaving the formants **barely move**, because they use a much smaller step to match the big values in hertz.

sections.title: Predict how changing a marked weight affects error

teaching.text: The same thing has to be asked about every weight, which is **whether the error will go up or down if this weight goes up**. The weights at the **end** of the network are much easier to change than those at the **beginning**.
**The end weights are easy because they directly change the decision.**
children: Done's probability comes partly from multiplying a positive end weight by a positive activation, along with the other products feeding done.
**If that end weight went up, done's probability would go up**, which is the exact opposite of what is needed.
So **that end weight should go down**, and any change to an end weight is **directly, automatically and immediately** reflected in the probabilities.

teaching.text: **The beginning weights are hard because their effect is buried under many layers.**
children: Changing a weight in the first layer changes that layer's **activations**, since activations are inner products of the weights with the inputs.
Those changed activations change the activations of the **next layer**, even with that layer's weights held fixed.
Those changes reach the **third layer**, and the third layer's changes finally reach the **probabilities**.

So **changing an early weight changes one thing, which changes another, which changes another, which finally changes the decision.** Just by looking at it, there is no way to tell which direction it should move, but backpropagation still figures it out.

teaching.text: **This is the same trap as the greedy choice in dynamic programming.** Picking the cheaper of two next steps without looking ahead can lead to the wrong answer, and in the same way, a weight's local appearance says little about its effect on the final decision.

sections.title: Backpropagation reuses downstream error calculations

teaching.text: **Dynamic programming says that if problems can be ordered by difficulty, the easiest should be solved first, then the next, and so on up to the hardest**, and backpropagation follows exactly that order.
**The last weights, W5, are the easiest problem.**
children: **The output probabilities are directly determined by the last weights**, so **the error is very directly determined by them** as well.
So the error can be used **right away** to decide how to change W5.

teaching.text: **The first weights, W2, are the hardest problem.**
children: **W2 affects its own activations, which then affect another two layers of activations along with many other weights.**
So it is **really hard to figure out how much blame W2 deserves** for a mistake made all the way at the end.
Moreover, **the effect of W2 on the error already includes the effect of W5**, because W5 is downstream of W2.

teaching.text: **Solving the end first makes the rest easier.** Changing the last weights first teaches something that makes the problem of the next layer easier, which makes the layer after it easy too, all the way back to the start, and that is exactly dynamic programming. So **backpropagation is Bellman and Viterbi's dynamic programming combined with SGD**, where SGD improves each weight a little at a time and dynamic programming says to go **from the end backward**.

**Backpropagation is central to the world right now**, because modern AI systems run it on enormous numbers of weights, step by step, for months. These ideas come from **physics** and are closely tied to the **dynamical systems** behind acoustics and masses and springs.

sections.title: Pair each recording with its target row

teaching.text: To train the network, it gets **two matrices**, which are **tables of numbers** with one row for each student recording.
children: The **input matrix, Formant_Inputs**, has two columns, and each row holds one recording's **F1 and F2**.
The **target matrix, TrueVowel_Outputs**, has five columns, and each row is a **one-hot answer**, with a one for the true vowel and a zero for the others, in the order done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.

**Each row in one table goes with the same row in the other**, so a row of the target with all zeros and a one in the Dan column tells the network that it should be completely sure that recording is Dan.
The rows on display are only a sample of the full set of recordings.

teaching.text: **Learning picks rows one at a time.**
children: It takes one row and uses its weights to calculate a decision for that row's formants.
If that decision differs from the desired answer, it **changes its weights**, the last ones first and then back toward the start.
It then picks another row and does the same thing again.

teaching.text: **If the network already gets a row right, there is no error, so there is nothing to learn from that row.** That can be a serious problem, because a network can make the right decision **by accident** over and over and stop learning early, without ever learning the **real pattern** underneath the data.
**Children learning English have the same problem**, as **Carol Chomsky** discovered.
children: At first, very young children say **"go"** and **"went"** correctly, because they are just **memorizing** what they hear.

Then they notice the real pattern, that most English verbs add **-ed** for the past, as in **jump, jumped** and **dance, danced**, and they start saying **"goed."** They have learned the rule, so they make **new mistakes**.
Only later do they learn that **some verbs are exceptions**, and then they get both the regular and the exceptional verbs right.
**Neural networks have the same issue**, because they can just **memorize** weights that give the right answers without learning the pattern, and that is what makes learning so difficult.

sections.title: Read one full-batch training step in PyTorch

teaching.text: A short **Python program** builds and trains the network. **It never has to be written from scratch**, and the brackets and dots do not matter, because what matters is **what the lines do**.
**The import lines bring in libraries.**
children: A **library** is a collection of programs that one group writes for one job and that others use without knowing how they work inside.
The lines **import torch** and **from torch import nn** **bring into Python everything needed for doing inner products, backpropagation and related work.**
Without libraries, the whole training program could never fit on one page.

teaching.text: The command **torch.load** **loads** the saved tables, the formants and the one-hot answers. Loading means bringing information in, the same thing that happens when a file is double-clicked, and **.float()** makes the values decimal numbers.

**The word Sequential means a neural network that is a sequence of layers.** All the networks built so far are a sequence of layers, while a **large language model** is a network that is **not** just a sequence of layers.

**Each Linear line is one processing layer**, meaning a layer that has weights and does **inner products** with the incoming information. **Linear means just use inner products**, so the formulas never have to be written out.
children: The first layer, **nn.Linear(2, 3)**, says that it receives information from **two** neurons and has **three** neurons of its own.
The next lines take **three and make two**, take **two and make four**, and take **four and make five**.
The network has **five layers but only four lines**, because the **input layer does no processing** and just receives the two formants.
No activation function sits between the layers, so the hidden layers are **linear**.

teaching.text: **The last lines are the only lines PyTorch needs for learning.**
children: The word **SGD** stands for **stochastic gradient descent**, and **lr** stands for the **learning rate**.
**A bigger learning rate learns a lot faster but is less accurate, while a smaller one is more accurate but learns much more slowly.**
The **loss** is **the mistake**, since the network calculates its mistakes and learns from them, and **CrossEntropyLoss** takes the raw scores and handles the probability part itself.
The command **zero_grad()** clears the old corrections, **backward()** is **backpropagation**, and **step()** changes the weights.
**Computing the corrections and changing the weights are separate steps**, so nothing changes until step() runs, and here all of the rows go through together for **one full step**.

teaching.text: The program starts from **PyTorch's own default weights and biases**, not the hand-picked weights in the diagram, so the structure matches but the numbers would not.

A short **Python program** builds and trains the network, and it never has to be written from scratch, since brackets and dots do not matter. **The import lines bring in libraries**, collections of programs that other people wrote for one job, which can be used without knowing how they work inside.
Before libraries like PyTorch existed, everyone doing AI had to write their own backpropagation code.
The import lines import into Python everything for doing inner products, backpropagation and related work, which is why the whole training program fits on one page.

**Sequential means a neural network that is a sequence of layers.** All the networks built so far are a sequence of layers, while a large language model is a network that is not just a sequence of layers. **Each Linear line is one processing layer**, a layer that has weights and does inner products with the incoming information.
The first linear line says it receives information from two neurons and has three neurons, and the following lines go from three to two, two to four, and four to five.
The network has five layers but only four lines, because the input layer does no processing.

**The last lines are the only lines PyTorch needs for learning.** SGD is stochastic gradient descent and lr is the learning rate, here 0.1. **A bigger learning rate learns a lot faster but is less accurate, while a smaller one is more accurate but learns much slower.**
Loss is the mistake, so the network calculates its mistakes and learns from them, and backward is backpropagation.
Nothing changes until step is called, which is when the weights actually change.

sections.title: Sigmoid turns an inner product into a bounded activation

teaching.text: **Neural networks do not come out of nowhere**, because their basic features come from **discoveries about animal brains**. Scientists found that brains have **neurons**, so networks have neurons, and they found that **each neuron collects information from many other neurons**, which is the **inner product**.

**Adrian** discovered that **neurons are nearly digital, because they either fire or they do not fire.** A real neuron's activation is not some in-between number, because it is basically **off or on**, while the neurons of the vowel network can take any value at all.

**The sigmoid** is an **activation function** that was added to networks to copy Adrian's discovery. It takes a neuron's **linear activation**, which is its inner product, and turns it into a number **between zero and one**. σ(z) = 1 / (1 + exp(-z))
children: Here z is the inner product, and σ(z) is the new activation.
**If the inner product is large and positive, the sigmoid is near one, and if it is large and negative, the sigmoid is basically zero.**

So a fairly negative inner product and a hugely negative one both come out near zero, a fairly positive one and a hugely positive one both come out near one, and only inner products close to zero land in between.
In this way **the sigmoid digitizes neural processing**, copying the brain chemistry that keeps real neurons close to off or on.

teaching.text: **The S shape changes how differences come out.** Near zero the curve is **steep**, so a small change in the inner product makes a big change in the output, while far from zero it is **flat**, so even big changes barely matter. **Animal perception reflects this, because some things that seem alike are perceived as different and some things that are very different are perceived as the same.**

**AI is duplicating the abilities of animals.** Engineers build in what biologists discover and then add their own ideas, so they might replace the sigmoid with other functions of a similar shape, such as **ReLU**. **People will say that AI has nothing to do with human cognition, but that is false**, because a big reason it works is that it copies our own abilities, using math as simple as multiplying and adding.

sections.title: Apply sigmoid while recalculating downstream activity

teaching.text: The sigmoid is added **one hidden neuron at a time**, while the input and every weight stay the same. The neurons switch in layer order, first the ones in the first hidden layer, then the second, then the third, and the outputs still use softmax.

The first neuron to switch has an inner product **just below zero**, which sits on the steep middle of the curve, so it comes out **just under one half**. The neuron now sends a **positive** number instead of a negative one.

**After each switch, everything downstream is recalculated**, because later neurons depend on earlier ones. So the sigmoid network cannot be made by running the old linear numbers through the sigmoid one at a time, since each new value has to come from the updated layer before it.

With **every hidden neuron on sigmoid**, every hidden activation sits between zero and one, and the answer moves completely. **Dan becomes the top answer**, **dean rises to second place**, and **done drops well behind**. **Only the activation rule changed and no weight moved, so this is not learning**, and even though the decision changed completely, **dean is still not the top answer**.

sections.title: Insert sigmoid after the hidden linear layers

teaching.text: The command **nn.Sigmoid()** is added after each of the first three Linear layers. **The command nn.Sigmoid means apply the sigmoid, which makes the neurons digital**, and the layer sizes stay exactly the same, because the sigmoid changes values but not how many there are.

**The last layer, nn.Linear(4, 5), has no sigmoid**, because its five scores go to the loss, which turns them into probabilities. The **sigmoid** squeezes **each hidden neuron on its own**, while the **softmax** turns **all five final scores together** into a decision that adds up to one.
The training lines and the learning rate stay the same. The program starts from PyTorch's default weights, so it would not reproduce the diagram's exact numbers.

sections.title: One initialization · training the linear network for 2,000 updates

teaching.text: Training runs **thousands of times**, which is far more than the few dozen steps needed to average a list of numbers, and **each full pass of learning is called an epoch.**
children: The starting weights are **random**, and that particular random set is called the **initialization**.
The network is linear, with no biases, and the formants are scaled down from hertz to kilohertz to keep the numbers small.

After every epoch, accuracy is measured without training. **The vowel with the largest score is the network's answer, and accuracy is the percentage of recordings it gets right**, and since these are the same recordings it learns from, this is called **training accuracy**.

teaching.text: **Accuracy starts at twenty percent, which is chance.**
children: At the start the weights are random, so the network knows nothing.
It still is not at zero, because with **five vowels**, a random guess is right **one time in five**.
The word **chance** means how often someone would be right just by guessing randomly, so **with five possible answers, chance is twenty percent.**

teaching.text: **After a couple hundred epochs, accuracy jumps up well above chance**, so the network is **learning something**. It dips back toward chance for a moment, recovers, and then levels off a little below half after a few hundred epochs.

sections.title: Ten initializations · different paths, the same final accuracy

teaching.text: The same training is run **ten times**, each time starting from **different random weights**, while everything else stays identical.
**The runs take different paths but end in the same place.**
children: All ten runs start near **twenty percent**, the level of chance.
Some leave chance quickly and others stay flat longer, and several briefly drop back toward chance.
After a few hundred epochs they **come together**, and **all ten finish at the same accuracy, a little below half**.
So **different starting weights change the path but not the destination**, because the learning process is so similar each time.

teaching.text: **The network levels off well below perfect accuracy because the data overlap so much.** Its final accuracy is clearly better than chance, so the network has learned something, but it is still pretty low.
children: **AI is not some kind of magic.** If a person had to name the vowel for formants landing where several vowels overlap, they would have to squint hard and might still guess wrong.
**If the decision is very hard for humans, it is not surprising that it is hard for machines.**
The limit comes from **two formants not being enough to separate dune, Don and done**, not from unlucky starting weights, so trying more starting points would not help.

teaching.text: **Different network designs can be tested in lab** by adding or removing layers, changing the number of neurons, or swapping in the sigmoid or other functions, and each change is checked for whether it **improves** that accuracy or makes it worse.

sections.title: NNs → LLMs → Agentic Systems
Neural networks, 1943–1986 · a static vector and a few categories

teaching.text: A **neural network** takes in information about **one moment**, uses its **weights** to process it, and makes a **decision**, and it learns those weights by **making errors and correcting them through backpropagation**. The vowel network is this kind of system, because it takes **two formants**, passes them through **three hidden layers**, and decides among **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
**The idea began with a paper by McCulloch and Pitts**, which proposed that simple mathematics could model how the brain works, and that paper described the first artificial neural network.
children: The paper starts from the **"all-or-none"** character of nervous activity, where **"all" means active and "none" means inactive**, so a neuron is either firing or not firing.

That is the same idea as the **sigmoid**, which pushes a neuron's activation toward off or on, so **the very first paper on artificial neural networks starts from biology about how real neurons behave.**
